utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier. Good morning, Your Honours. I wish to start my closing arguments by briefly mentioning the Prosecution witnesses and, more specifically, those who came from Bosnia in order to testify before you. It is through them that we've heard what happened on the 16th of April in Ahmici. It is mainly through their testimony that we've heard about the massacre. Prosecution witnesses, unlike Defence witnesses, have, for most of them before they testified in Court, made written statements. Often they made several recent statements at various times. All of them, and it is quite legitimate, were faced here with their written statements and it sometimes happened that their credibility was challenged. And no matter what the feelings may have been that have been aroused by those witnesses in this courtroom and among the judges, I believe that one thing will have been demonstrated, is that these witnesses from Bosnia did not together plot against the truth but, in the contrary, all of them came from Bosnia in order to help justice and to manifest the truth regarding their community, their family, their next of kins, their lives. I shall add, at the beginning of my closing arguments, that I feel that the accused themselves did not help the truth to be established. Some of them, and I have in mind those who testified before you, some of them acknowledge that a very serious matter had been committed in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. They acknowledged that a certain amount of non-combatants were killed, but I do not have the feeling, and reading the written conclusions of the Defence does confirm that, I don't have the feeling that they -- the accused gave up the allegations of a fight, of an armed resistance taking place in Ahmici, as though the resistance opposed by the victim could count to mitigation for the attackers. One thing is certain, at the end of this trial, as was obvious before the trial even began; one thing is obvious: The operation engaged in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, whatever its nature, maybe is today not claimed by a single person. And if we think that if there was a fight, it was a doubtful one. If it was a victory through arms, it was a shameful victory. No order was issued to order the operation and there is no account for it anywhere. In my closing arguments I shall first speak to the attack directed by the HVO forces on the 16th of April, '93 against the Muslim civil population of Ahmici. And I think it is important to state the figures, the numbers. And then coming to the legal questions and to the law applied by this Tribunal, I should like to define the characteristics of the attack directed against the Muslim population in Ahmici. I shall then turn to the evidence gathered during the trial against every one of the accused. And finally, I shall present recommendations as to sentencing, appropriate sentencing for each of the accused. In order to attempt to be as close to the truth as possible regarding the attack against the population in Ahmici, I think it is most legitimate to speak of individual tragedies. Of course there are as many tragedies as there are victims. But some of the testimony we've heard here in this courtroom, more than others, have made it possible to grasp the horror of what happened in Ahmici on the 16th of April, to flesh it out and to give it its full meaning. In very few words I shall speak of three people who came to testify here. Let us start with Witness D, who testified on the 26th of August, 1998. You will remember this Muslim woman, a mother, devout, no doubt. She lived in Lower Ahmici, close to the main road and to the Catholic cemetery. This witness told us she woke up very early for prayers. Her husband left for the mosque Around 5.20, as was the case for all witnesses. She heard shooting directed at the house. Together with her daughter, her two sons, she tried to seek shelter. A soldier came into the house, forced the son, the oldest son, to leave through the first floor balcony. The son was forced to jump, and as soon as he fell he was shot dead. The younger son was forced to jump as well, but he was able to escape. Then the soldier forced the witness out on the balcony. She saw her son lying dead with blood all over his head. She saw soldiers lower down. The attacker ordered her to jump from the balcony while other soldiers were laughing. And she was able to see her son lying dead on the ground. The witness would not jump. She was overwhelmed by horror. And in Court she said this, in order to describe the soldier facing her, "This beast in front of me, senseless, he would do whatever he wanted. He knew no limit." And indeed the attackers on the 16th of April, '93 in Ahmici knew no limit. They could kill a young man, forgive another one. They had full power of death and life over people who were disarmed, over women, children, over families, over a whole community. The testimony of Witness F, who testified here on the 31st of August, 1998, made it possible for us to understand what the fate was of children in the midst of this tragedy. Witness F was then only 15 years old. He lived in a house close to the lower mosque, together with his parents, his 8-year-old brother, and his 4-year-old sister. When the house was besieged, the father was not there. The door of the house was broken down by the soldiers. A grenade was thrown inside the house; it rolled towards the mother. She grabbed the grenade in order to try and throw it outside; the grenade exploded. The mother was wounded, whilst the small brother, the little brother, was killed. Another grenade exploded in the house, wounding the witness in the legs, but she was still able to seek shelter in a room. A soldier came into the house, threw another grenade, and, as was told by the witness, he was in a camouflage uniform, had black paint over his face, the HVO insignia, and coloured ribbons at the shoulder. Other grenades were thrown inside the house. The house was in flames. At the request of his mother, the witness dragged the body of the young brother outside the house. The mother was hit in the stomach. The witness sought shelter in a barn close to the house. He dragged the body of the brother there, and he took the little sister there. The mother, crawling on the ground, managed to get there. The witness closed the barn door. Half an hour later, his mother was dead. Throughout the day, throughout the following night, he was going to protect his sister by putting her in a concrete trough. On several occasions he fainted, because he lost a lot of blood. In the night, soldiers tried to break into the barn. They managed to open the door slightly, throw a grenade inside, shooting inside as well. Using a torch, they could see the body of the mother, of the little brother, of the radio. They sent a message to the authorities to say that everything had been killed around the mosque. The next day, the witness left the barn in order to seek something to eat and he saw bodies all around him, the corpses of some of his neighbours, among whom Husein Ahmic and the lifeless body of his neighbour, Witness G. He could see Melissa, who is 7, lying next to her dead mother. When he asked her to come along, she said that she didn't want to go because her mother was sleeping, she wanted to stay next to her. Later on, the witness was taken to the Dubravica school, where he was detained until the 1st of May. In the meantime, a Croat soldier stole the money he was able to rescue from the fire from him. The testimony of Witness K was, I think, one of the most moving testimonies we've heard here. You will remember that Witness K lived in Grabovi, a little higher than the Kupreskic houses. She lived in that house, together with her husband, her son, who was ten, and her two daughters, four and six. The family was woken up by shooting directed at the house. Bullets came through the windows. The noise was deafening; they couldn't hear each other speak to one another. The mother tried to protect her children. She was afraid that grenades would be thrown into the room. She begged that her children be spared. She told us that at a point in time, her son wanted to go and have a pee. He insisted; therefore, she let him go towards the sink in the kitchen. From the kitchen, her son said, "I'm wounded," showing his arm. His father then opened the door, the main door, and shouted towards the soldiers, "You wounded my child." Outside, the witness saw a soldier; he was a fair-haired man with a gun. He ordered the husband to leave, to come out. The husband took his child, the son, in his arms, shouting again, "You hurt, you wounded my son," in his bare feet, in his pyjamas. Some two or three metres outside the front door, the father and the son were shot dead together through one burst of automatic rifle. The mother went back in in order to protect her daughters. Around the house, this shooting, running, shouting. The mother went out again; she wanted to see her son again. She looked at him and she told us, "I realised he had been wounded on the right side, not on the left side." However, she knew that he was dead. She dragged him back into the house, kept watching over her children, trying to help her husband. She said, and I shall quote her, "I didn't know what to do. I was absolutely panicked. I would pace up and down, go from one window to the other. I couldn't cry. There were no tears. I would drink water. I would pour water over my nape, my head, not to faint; to hold on." Outside, she could see the burning houses, the corpses of her Muslim neighbours, among which the body of a woman who was 74 years old. She sought shelter. She hid her two daughters. In the afternoon, she was able to go to Vrhovine. We all know that testifying before a criminal court is only an imperfect way of accounting for a crime. It doesn't give back the noise, the furor of the attacker, the panic of the victims. Through such testimony, I believe that some of this very basic, substantial truth about the massacre has been given back to us. At the end of that day of the 16th of April, 1993, as the final sign of their victory over the civilian victims, over those families surprised in the middle of the night, as the culmination of their criminal intent, as a confession, they blew up the concrete minaret of the lower mosque. Towards Upper Ahmici, their work has been mopped up. Those who didn't want to flee, who couldn't flee, were killed in their houses. Witnesses Q and S told this Tribunal that their mother and father, who were 83 and 78 years old, who were unable to flee, were killed, like other people, in Upper Ahmici. If we don't know for sure the number of victims, at least we have some idea. Witness S, who knew all the Ahmici inhabitants very well, having lived there his entire life, drafted a list of those who were killed during the attack. We know, and I think that this is not challenged by the Defence, we know that if there were 600 inhabitants in Ahmici before the 16th of April, after that date there was not a single one left. So 116 people were accounted as being killed, including 28 women and 16 children or adolescents. Of the 116 victims, barely half of them were men of fighting age, but it was not established during the trial that any of them were killed with a weapon in his hand. In addition, we were told that at that time in Ahmici, there were a certain number of refugees living, that is, Muslim refugees. Not everybody knew them. We don't know the exact number of them today, as we do not know the number of victims among them who fell. We also know that 24 people were wounded during the attack, about one-third of whom were children. And, of course, this does not really count all the victims, because the victims, there are those who lost relatives, lost their homes, their lands, and their property. Everyone who met the survivors of Ahmici in the days or weeks following the attack, while they were being temporarily lodged in some sort of collection centre, described their distress, their anguish, their physical and moral misery, and some of them did receive some psychological support or some psychiatric treatment, but there are many of them who were not able to have a normal life again after that date. Some of those who died in Ahmici were buried in Vitez on the 28th of April, 1993, and the Trial Chamber remembers that the witness, Stephen Hughes, who was a member of the British Battalion, was present at the burial of 96 bodies of Muslims who had been exchanged for three bodies of Croats. The witness Nihad Rebihic, who was responsible for the collective burial, told the Tribunal what happened. It was established that the bodies that were buried on the 28th of April in Vitez came from several locations in the Vitez region. It was not possible to identify all of them, but it seems that 70 to 80 of the bodies that were buried that day came from Ahmici. These are bodies of men, women, of all ages. Two bodies only of the bodies that were buried that day were wearing uniforms. The Prosecution has submitted to the Tribunal death certificates for '93. Several families still do not know where their dead are resting. Thus, Witness R and her sister, Witness T, do not know where their mother is buried, their mother who was killed, in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house. The witness told the Tribunal that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic's brother-in-law had come to suggest that one of them -- come to tell one of them where the place of the burial was, so long as they would not testify in this trial. That individual is referring to the Red Cross, which of course obviously was a way of trying to make the records not clear, because the Red Cross had absolutely nothing to do with the burials of the victims in Ahmici. And under those conditions we know that there are still in Ahmici, in the surroundings of Ahmici, there are common graves which are clandestine. As regards the number of houses involved in the attack, we know that 169 homes were destroyed deliberately in Ahmici and Santici and Pirici, 102 homes in Ahmici alone. And we also know that the two mosques in Ahmici were deliberately destroyed. Now, in order, to speak about law. I would like to refer to the characteristics of that which allow us to classify it as a crime. I would like to say first that the attack on the 16th of April, 1993 is a well-thought-out action, perfectly organised from a technical point of view. Obviously, it was not a spontaneous event of a unit which had gone out of all control. Much to the contrary, it is a coordinated attack of various units who were placed under the same operational leadership, using, from one end to the other of the village, the same procedures. We know that the attackers deployed at 5.20 in the morning, at the time when the call to prayer had been given from the mosque. For some time heavy weapons had been put into positions on the periphery of the village and we also know that the attackers were in positions in several locations in the village, particularly near the Catholic cemetery, in Grabovi, and on the side of the house where Drago Josipovic and Dragan Papic live, and the attack was deployed simultaneously from those three points. We know that the homes occupied by the Muslim families were all attacked by well-armed soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms or in black uniforms, as described by many of the witnesses. We know some of them were wearing hoods or black paint on their faces. Different types of weapons were used. There were anti-aircraft guns, there were rocket launchers, there were sub-machine guns. The significance of these weapons implies orders and war logistics. And the Jokers, acting alone, obviously would not have been able to implement all this by themselves. Everywhere, from one end of the village to the other, the houses are fired on. Grenades are thrown through openings. Families are ordered to get out of their homes. Some of the men were shot on the spot, sometimes children. Others died as they attempted to flee. As soon as the homes were destroyed by incendiary assets, all of the homes and all of the outbuildings and the property of the Muslims, specifically livestock, because some of the attackers also became involved in plunder. The numbers of people that were involved were obviously much greater than those of a squad, because from several homes there were simultaneous attacks carried out by five or six soldiers. There were many of these soldiers and therefore they had to have been coordinated. They had radio communication assets, they had colour ribbons on their shoulders. They were prepared. They had objectives which had been assigned to them. They knew which houses had to be destroyed and which houses were not to be destroyed. They knew the names of the heads of the families, sometimes their first names. Several witnesses that this Tribunal heard said that the Croatian soldiers would mention -- orders that they had received that they had to obey. And sometimes they heard them congratulating one another because everything has gone according to plan. The point of view of Major Dooley was that the operation was conducted from the beginning to the end in a military fashion by various units which were coordinated amongst themselves and directed by somebody who had control and mastery of tactical issues. In the absence of resistance, it would not take the HVO forces a long time to reach their goals. At around noon, most likely, as Major Dooley said to us, the operation was concluded in Lower Ahmici and in Grabovi. We also know that 150 to 200 people, all of them Muslims, including a large -- a great majority of the women and children and some older people, some of whom came from Ahmici and others from other villages in the Lasva Valley, were detained from the 16th of April, or that is after the 16th of April, until the 1st of May, within the Dubravica school. They were detained and guarded by the armed HVO forces. And it was very clear that the detention could not have been improvised. Several witnesses also told us that during the detention women were mistreated and assaulted sexually. The first characteristic of the attack was that it was very carefully prepared and organised and that it involved significant assets in respect of materiel and men. The second character of that attack is that because there was a military objective, this action was carried out against the civilian population. We do not have any indications of a Muslim military presence in Ahmici on the 16th of April, despite the efforts which the Defence made in order to show that there was. Major Dooley confirmed that in April 1993 the Army of Bosnia was practically absent from the Vitez-Ahmici region. Witness AA, who at the time was a member of the military police under the orders of the accused Vladimir Santic, said that he never saw Bosnian army forces in Ahmici. Therefore, there is no defence which was organised on the part of the village. Major Dooley saw no sign of resistance. The victims were all civilians, men and women. And none of those individuals was armed. We also know that the Territorial Defence in Ahmici at that time was not a force of a military nature which would be possible to put up resistance or any opposition. In the beginning of 1993, Territorial Defence in Ahmici, there were about 20 civilians. They might have had some military obligations, but when they were in Ahmici, in their families, their activity was limited to moving around at night in the village in order to ensure that their homes were protected, that their neighbourhoods and families were protected as well. Their organisation was really embryonic. Many of them, overly confident, did not take these guard duties seriously and tried not to go on guard duty; and therefore, on the part of the members of that Territorial Defence, there was very little engagement and very little discipline. In Ahmici there are no military facilities, no barracks, no defence set-up and no storage for military materiel, and therefore during these proceedings, this trial, the Defence was unable to prove that there had been a battle pitting the armed forces, one against the other, nor was it able to understand that there had been a legitimate attack in principle, or even mere resistance on the part of the Muslims, resistance to the attack against them. Colonel Watters, in his testimony, stated that this was the first battlefield that he had been given the opportunity to see where no dead soldier was to be seen and where obviously all of the victims were civilians. The third characteristic is that this civilian population is Muslim. There was much corroborating testimony pointed out that apparently there were racist insults made against their victims, and especially the use of the word balija, which is a pejorative classification for Muslims which the Croats used. Therefore, it is clear that the victims of the attack were targeted only because they were not Croats, but Muslims, and that their houses were destroyed because that is where Muslim families lived. A few minutes ago I mentioned the large number of houses that had been destroyed. I must also say that all the Muslim houses in Ahmici were destroyed, as were the outbuildings and livestock. And the most evident result of this attack is the fact that of the 600 Muslim residents in Ahmici, not one is left after the 16th of April. It was an entire community which was wiped off that location, and all trace of its existence was erased and any possibility of a retort was deliberately destroyed. On the contrary, the Croat community in Ahmici is intact. It was established that not a single Croat civilian was hit, killed or even wounded; that there was no damage made to Croat property in Ahmici, no Catholic religious symbol was hit or degraded. The members of the British Battalion were struck, and they told so in Court by the discrepancy, by the fact that the destruction in the village was obviously targeted by the quasi-surgical character of this operation, which wanted to exclude a religious and cultural -- a political committee out of a territory. I know that all the accused tried to establish that their house had been hit or looted. I think that in doing so they wanted to show that they -- their fate was that of the Muslim victims, but it is obvious that not even the beginning of evidence has been produced to show so. It was not established either that the Croats had military loss, however limited, on the 16th of April in Ahmici. We had long discussions revolving around this issue and we know today for certain that two people were wounded that belonged to the Croat forces, and there were only two, Nikola Omazic and Ivica Semren. The last aspect of the operation directed against Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993 that is worth underlining is the fact that this operation is to be seen within the wider framework of a general assault, a military assault with political aims. Admittedly, because of the geographical extent of the village, because of the number of victims in the village, because of the heavy damage caused and the large amount of military means implemented, shows in itself that it is a large-scale crime. But it is worth showing also that Ahmici is not a single, isolated fact, because other Muslim villages in the Lasva Valley were then in the following days attacked. And all those attacks were pursuing the same goal, that of ethnic cleansing. Such attacks are to be seen within the framework of a deliberate, wilful policy, which is to take over the power, the HVO to take over the power in Central Bosnia. During this trial, through Prosecution evidence, but also through some Defence witness testimony, we have adduced a large amount of evidence about this political and military situation. We were informed of the development as of November 1991 of the movements of the Bosnian Croats, of its political and territorial claims. These claims or objectives were to have an autonomous territory, which was a first step towards sovereignty. Croats gave themselves an army, an army which was equipped. The Croat and Muslim communities parted and got further away from each other. As to the HVO, it gradually took power over all aspects of civilian, social and economic life. Tensions between the communities, communities which were allied against the Serb aggressor, such tensions exacerbated to lead to the October '92 events in Ahmici, which is a clear sign of it. The Prosecution does not challenge, it even holds it for established, that members of the Croat community in Central Bosnia were too victims of atrocities. It happened in other places in the Lasva Valley, not on the 16th of April, but prior to or possibly after the 16th of April. I have in mind the testimony of Zeljka Rajic on the 27th of January, who told us what happened in Dusina in January '93. But it is obvious that no crime can be justified by another crime. But it is equally clear that in the Lasva Valley during the time prior to the 16th of April, 1993, as far as the Muslim community was concerned, the insecurity kept rising. We saw much evidence of that throughout the trial. I have one thing in mind in particular. It is Prosecution Exhibit 352. It was a video film shot by the Croat propaganda which shows us in the middle of Ahmici two soldiers in black uniforms demonstrating shooting skills whilst a journalist or reporter, if that is a reporter, has threatening comments towards the Muslims. We had many signs of the war preparations carried out by the Croat community in Central Bosnia, or at least by the authorities, the HVO authorities. I remember, in particular, all the orders issued by the Operative Zone command, Blaskic, as of 1993, January 1993 up to April 1993. Colonel Watters testified as to the general character of the offensive carried out by the Croats on the 16th of April. Firing or shooting started in Vitez at the same time as it started in Ahmici. The way he described Vitez on the 16th of April at 8.30 is that of a battlefield, where all the victims are civilians. The testimony of Major Dooley and of Stephen Hughes corroborate his testimony. Throughout the valley, Muslim houses can be seen torched. All the Muslim civilians have to flee or else they're killed, arrested, taken to camps, such as the Kaonik camp, or other detention centres. A truck bomb exploded, as you remember, on the 18th of April in Stari Vitez. Six people are killed, eight seriously wounded. The perpetrators of this attack want to terrorise the Muslim civilian population, force it to leave the city, leave the valley. The Zenica shelling on the 19th of April by the HVO is triggered by the same logics of terror. Colonel Watters told us that the Croats had used this window of opportunity that had opened then, since the Muslim forces were busy on the western front against the Serbs and since the media was busy because of the events then taking place in Srebrenica. Due to the character, the type of attack, it can be characterised as a crime. We know that the perpetrators are Bosnian Croats, that they acted deliberately, systematically, fully aware of the goals they were pursuing. We know that they wanted to achieve the ethnic cleansing of the Ahmici village and all of the various locations in the Lasva Valley. We know that their attack was directed against a civilian population which was unarmed, undefended, and we know that the civilian population was a Muslim population by culture, tradition, and religion. We know that during the attack many civilians were murdered, that their property was destroyed, and that the survivors had to leave their land, and we obviously can see that this attack is part of an armed conflict between the HVO and the military means at the disposal of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, this attack can only be qualified in one way: as a crime against humanity. Let me now turn to the part played by the Croat residents in Ahmici, before we turn to each and every accused. We know that prior to the war, there was coexistence between the communities, that they sometimes were on good terms and, anyway, were always on peaceful terms with one another. But we also know that as of 1991, the relationship started deteriorating. The Croat media, radio and television started broadcasting propaganda. The nationalistic feelings started developing among the Croats. They had the feeling that they were Catholics and Croats before they were Bosnians, and they had the feeling that they did not belong to the same national community as the Muslims, which led them to want to separate from them. Several witnesses described this process of separation leading to disaster. I have, in particular, in mind Professor Tone Bringa. Some witnesses minced facts that apparently were without any relevance. There were new words that cropped up in the vocabulary used by Bosnian Croats, for instance. But when you put all this together, when you piece it together, then the story gets its meaning. There is one thing that is specific to Ahmici. It was said by many witnesses, including Defence witnesses, it is due to the influx of Muslim refugees to Ahmici, whilst the Croat refugees from the front line did not settle in the Vitez area but carried on on their way. As a result, so it seems for the Croats living in the Ahmici area, it gave rise to a worrying situation. I remember that Ivica Kupreskic said that the Ahmici population doubled in size because of the influx of refugees, who were all Muslims. Against this background and this process of separation of communities, we saw that armed forces of the HVO appeared within the village of Ahmici. One should stop for a moment to consider what the HVO was at that period of time. During the hearings, we referred at length to regulations and laws, but at this stage of the hearings, I wish to focus on three ideas. The first is that in the circumstances at the time, the operative reality preceded the administrative reality. I remember that Witness DA for the Defence, who was in charge of the administration and the reorganisation of the Vitez Brigade, confirmed this; the witness admitted that the Vitez Brigade existed on the ground before it existed administratively. The second idea is that as soon as the Croatian community thought it was in jeopardy, there was no difference between those in reserve and active-duty soldiers. The third idea was the contradiction between active and non-active and it was replaced by the opposition between a voluntary and a professional member of personnel. In 1992 and 1993, the Croats of Bosnia were living through a period of revolution. What I mean is that they were trying to establish a new national and political order, built on the ruins of a former order, and under those circumstances, the real and the former could no longer coincide. One did not reflect the other. Furthermore, the Croats were not numerous or thought they were not numerous. All of them were mobilised, in fact, and the mobilisation, in the name of an allegedly threatened community, was effective before it became official. For example, Rudo Vidovic, a restaurant owner in Zume, declared that many times, even though he did not officially belong to HVO forces, he went to fight the Serbs on Mount Vlasic in 1992, and he also said that his son did the same on a number of occasions. The witness described this as a widespread practice. Some went to the front in civilian clothing, others in camouflage uniform. Milutin Vidovic, again for the Defence, declared that twice in 1992, on the front against the Serbs, for two periods of seven days each, as a voluntary soldier, he went there without being officially a member of the HVO. The same applies to (redacted) and Ivo Pranjkovic, who was a reservist and who went to the front line at Kuber on the 13th of April, 1993. Also this applies to Witness Andjelko Vidovic, who also told us that he went to Kuber on this same date, the 13th of April, 1993. Let us also recall Stipo Alilovic, who left Bosnia to go to Holland on the 29th of March, 1992 and who stated to the Dutch authorities, in support of his request for refugee status, that he had to leave Bosnia because he was summoned to join the army of the Croats of Bosnia. Let us also recall that in his order, dated the 16th of January, 1993, Colonel Blaskic ordered the combat readiness of the HVO to be raised to the highest level, that all armed members of the Croatian people should be included in HVO units. We must assume that certain consequences followed from this order, which signified, at the same time, a levy, en masse, of the Croats of Bosnia and their combat orders. Goran Males, who testified for the Defence, and who was a professional soldier, admitted that at the time there was no major difference between the position of a reservist and an active-duty soldier. In fact, there were no reservists because the Croats were too few. The register of the HVO, of the HVO soldiers, makes a distinction between professionals and reservists; it does not make a distinction between active duty and reserve duty. All non-professional soldiers are reservists, whether they are active duty or not. This HVO, which, from the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, is everywhere, it is also present, of course, in Ahmici. The 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade was responsible for a zone which includes Ahmici. Its commander is Slavko Papic, who was frequently cited during our hearings. According to many witnesses, in particular, Defence witnesses, he was present in Ahmici on the 16th of April, as of 4.00 in the morning, and the next day. I am referring, in particular, to the testimony of Milutin Vidovic. What is known as the Home Guards also existed in Ahmici. They were certainly still not administered, but they had a commander, Nenad Santic, who is named in an order dated 12th March 1993. Nenad Santic was, indeed, a prominent figure at that period, as numerous prosecution, as well as Defence, witnesses have underlined. He issued orders of a military nature and, particularly, according to the testimony of Dragan Papic himself, the Croatian forces were under the instructions of the commander of the operational zone. Let us recall that Witness Zvonimir Santic, called by the Defence, who is not from Ahmici but from Rovna, stated that the village guards of Donja Rovna received, before the attack of the 16th of April, an order to guard the Radak Bridge from the headquarters of the HVO in Busovaca. Under these conditions, do we have indicators and evidence of what the members of the Croatian community in Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici were in any way involved, in a passive or active manner, in the attack conducted against the Muslims? It is obviously a difficult question of this trial, and of course I will state my views with a great deal of caution. The Defence claimed that forces came from outside, that an independent unit, which was not part of the regular HVO forces, arrived, but the defendants themselves did incriminate themselves. It should be noted that the only losses that were suffered were among the inhabitants of Ahmici, and Mirjan Santic, Nikola Omazic, and Ivica Semren were Croats, the latter two belonging to regular units of the HVO. The regular army of the HVO was present in Ahmici, and the residents of Ahmici had their role there. A second observation: The attackers were perfectly well-informed. They knew who lived where; they knew that this house was Muslim, another Croat, even though no external difference allowed one to distinguish between them. But the attackers did not make a single error because not a single Croatian house was destroyed. I should like to recall that several witnesses said that the attackers knew the first and last names of their victims. A third observation: The Croatian residents of Ahmici were informed in advance and they evacuated. Several Prosecution witnesses said that the 15th of April was a rather unusual day. Witness A saw Dragan Papic leave in a red Lada with his family towards Busovaca and return alone half an hour later without his family. Witness F also saw, on the afternoon of the 15th of April, this red Lada of the Papic family leave, with women and children inside; this car returned later with other people inside. This same witness, Witness F, in the course of that same afternoon, also saw Ivica Kupreskic at the steering wheel of his Mercedes leaving Ahmici with his family. Witness Fahrudin Ahmic saw Vinko Vidovic on the 15th of April in the evening, together with his wife and children, preparing to leave in a car in the direction of Busovaca. Witness F and G told the Tribunal that Croatian children, their school friends, were absent on the Thursday of the 15th of April, 1993. A fourth observation: We know that upon the initiative of Nenad Santic, a meeting was held in the night between the 15th and the 16th of April, attended by several inhabitants of Ahmici. I should like to refer to the testimony of Dragan Vidovic, who said that around 2.30 or 3.00 in the morning, he was called on the phone by Nenad Santic, who asked him to go to the house of Witness (redacted). He there found other Croat residents of Ahmici; he mentions their names in the course of his testimony. According to this witness, reference is made to an imminent attack of Muslim forces, and the witness is asked to awaken a certain number of people. According to Dragan Vidovic, who declared this during the examination-in-chief and also during the cross-examination, (redacted) was also present at the meeting, son of (redacted), who later died. We know through another witness, Zvonimir Cilic, that (redacted) was probably a member of the military police. It is this man that Witness EE said he saw in front of his door on the 16th of April, in the morning, accompanied by Vlado Santic and Drago Josipovic. It is (redacted) who spoke during this meeting and who issued instructions. We must ask ourselves what he might have said to these Croatian inhabitants of Ahmici. A fifth observation has to do with the very limited and localised scope of the evacuation. In reality, this evacuation, regardless of the moment it took place, whether it was on the eve or early in the morning of the 16th of April, affected only the Croats living among Muslims; for example, the Kupreskics but not the Sakics. And if, as the accused claimed, there was fear of a Mujahedin attack on the village, Mujahedin coming from the north, from the mountains, then obviously all the Croatian houses would be at risk. Finally, I should like to refer to the testimony of Professor Tone Bringa on the basis of his experience from another area, which resembles Ahmici, and who told us that, according to information communicated to her, the attack against this village was prepared from the outside but that certain Croat inhabitants of the village participated in it in a similar process to the one that took place in Ahmici. Consequently, the Prosecution says that the community of Croats in Ahmici could not and was not uninformed about what was brewing, that some inhabitants of Ahmici were associated with the attack that was being prepared and participated in it. I would now like to mention the evidence which has been adduced against the -- each of the accused, and start with the accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. I am going to examine their situation together, because it seems to me that on the ground and also within this trial, to a large extent they have linked their fate, and the review of the facts in fact does show that they were in fact inseparable. The Prosecution states that the evidence that was brought to this Tribunal to show that the accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic actively engaged in the attack against the Muslim civilian population in Ahmici, that they actively contributed to the HVO's achieving its military and political objectives, and that they were also the direct perpetrators of the destruction of Witness KL's family. The first element that I would like to bring out to this Tribunal against the two accused is that both of them are implicated in the HVO armed forces. Zoran Kupreskic and his brother Mirjan both received military training within the former Yugoslav army. Both of them were seen by many witnesses before the 16th of April, 1993 in uniforms and armed, coming and going in the village of Ahmici. Witness S, for instance, Witness T, Witness V, frequently saw Zoran moving around in HVO uniform and carrying a weapon. The same holds for Mirjan Kupreskic, with one reservation, however; that is, Mirjan appeared less frequently in a uniform than did his brother. But Witness Z states that shortly after the events of October 1992, he participated at a checkpoint that was set up at the entrance of Ahmici, together with, among other people, Mirjan Kupreskic, who was wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying an automatic rifle. Moreover, during his testimony, the accused Zoran Kupreskic did not deny that he was able to move about in the village wearing a uniform, wearing his brother's camouflage jacket, and he did not deny the fact that he could carry out the armed guard and that he was armed with an automatic AK-47 weapon. Witness JJ, who perhaps even today had a very close friendship with the accused Zoran Kupreskic, and who worked in the same company as did the accused, declared formally that Zoran Kupreskic, before the 16th of April, 1993, was a member of the HVO. And she said that she had personally seen that Zoran Kupreskic would go to the front line against the Serbs; that he did not hide that fact; that it was normal for a Croat. Witness Abdulah Ahmic confirmed also that Zoran, as far as he knew, would often go to the front line. And this idea of a voluntary and temporary engagement on the front line for the Croats is something which we saw during these proceedings on several occasions. We learned that, according to Witness JJ, Zoran Kupreskic personally, while wearing a uniform, took an oath of allegiance to the HVO during a ceremony which took place at the Vitez city stadium, and that this ceremony, obviously, had a nationalistic characteristic and one of mobilisation as well. Although several Defence witnesses, I remember, denied that the ceremonies had ever taken place, the accused Zoran Kupreskic recognised that -- acknowledged, rather, that he had participated in one of these, but in public and wearing civilian clothes. And he was unable to explain to the Tribunal, it seems, why and how his friend could have made such a serious mistake. The names of the witnesses or the accused Zoran and Mirjan appear both in the HDZ and the HVO registers, which implies that there was an old and close association, both on a political and military level with the Bosnian Croats. I would remind you that these two documents are numbered 371 and 353. I would say that in this respect it is odd that we did not receive from the Defence Zoran's military booklet, nor did we receive Mirjan's, which is different in respect of the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic. The accused told us that the book exists but that each of them allegedly lost his own, but neither of them had lost his demobilisation certificate. Several Prosecution witnesses say that according to their own observations and experience, Zoran Kupreskic was not only an HVO soldier, he also held a rank in it. Abdulah Ahmic said that Zoran Kupreskic was the HVO Commander in Grabovi and that frequently he saw him wearing a uniform and arm, and would specifically see him together with Slavko Papic, another HVO commander, as seemed from what some of the Defence witnesses themselves said. Witness Y stated that there was a meeting held a few days before the attack of April 1993, which was called by Zoran Kupreskic, about the question of guards. It was presided over by Zoran Kupreskic. During the meeting the Croatian party wanted the guards set up by the Muslims -- stop operating within the village, and the Muslims proposed that they have joint patrols. And Zoran refused the compromise, and to justify his refusal he mentioned orders that he had received. According to the witness, Zoran on that occasion told those people he was speaking to that he was going to take up a new command and that his responsibilities in Ahmici would be carried out by somebody else. The protocol of 21 October 1992, which is Exhibit D27, is one of the pieces of evidence regarding the important role that Zoran Kupreskic played within the HVO structures and locally within the Croatian community in Ahmici. The document indicates what the conclusions for the negotiations were for the return of Muslim refugees. What did it mean? It meant that the Muslims -- the Muslims in Ahmici would surrender. First of all, it was established under the auspices of the HVO. Secondly, it prescribed the disarmament of the Ahmici Muslims. And thirdly, through this document, the HVO, as a counterpart of disarmament, guaranteed security for the Muslims. We know that this document was in fact used and it should be associated with the statements of the witness Abdulah Ahmic and those of the Witness U. Disarmament, of course, did take place, even though evidently it was not total. We could remember that Fahrudin Ahmic, who would see his weapons confiscated by Nenad Santic, who would then give it or have it given to Drago Josipovic. However, we know what would become of the guarantees promised by those who had signed the document. It appears clearly that the disarmament of the Muslims in Ahmici, in accordance with that order, was only able to facilitate the attack carried out on the 16th of April, 1993. The accused Zoran Kupreskic explained that it was written as it was being dictated to him, that he was the meeting secretary, and that he did not in any way really participate in that decision-making process, but all the other signatories of the document are dead and, therefore, he did not take the risk of -- did not run the risk of being challenged. Witness B, however, says what the real role of Zoran Kupreskic was in those negotiations. He told us that the day after the first conflict of October 1992, he met Nenad Santic in order to negotiate the return of the Muslim refugees, and with Nenad Santic he went to Zoran Kupreskic's house. Zoran Kupreskic, in front of him, took -- made commitments in the name of the Croatian community. He guaranteed the safety of the Muslim refugees when they came back and asserted that there would be no problem. Witness JJ stated that ten days before the conflict of April 1993, his friend Zoran told him that he was a local HVO Commander in Ahmici. She added that in the preceding days, the days preceding the 16th of April, Zoran mentioned in front of her a checkpoint which had been set up by the Muslims in Ahmici in order to prevent Dario Kordic from coming into the village. And Zoran said that he had been able to negotiate the dismantling of that roadblock without any difficulty. And that, I think, explains or can be explained by the fact that Zoran was in a position to extend his protection to his friend Witness JJ. And according to that witness's testimony, apparently, his name in and of itself represented a safe conduct. And that the name of Zoran Kupreskic was respected by soldiers, even though the statement that was signed by Marijan Skopljak was considered to be valueless by those very same soldiers. We, the Prosecution, in the proceedings established that the two accused, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, had played an active role and a conscious role in the attack of the 16th of April against the Muslim civilian population in Ahmici. And the Prosecution, in order to establish this, based itself on the following elements: I said that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic each were members, and active members, of the HVO, and as such they can only be associated, and as soon as it was conceived, in an operation carried out by the HVO on the village in which they lived, and that, in my opinion, the contrary -- the opposite would simply be inconceivable. The second element. We know that war preparations were being taken around the Kupreskic houses. Witness V stated on the 15th of April, 1993, in late afternoon, while he was riding around in a car, he saw between the houses of Ivica and Zoran Kupreskic about a dozen soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms and carrying weapons, as well as two civilians. This group of people worried him and he spoke about it immediately to some of his friends, which he confirmed when he testified before the Tribunal. And he said that there were -- from what he saw on the 16th of April, that is, the materiel and the soldiers there, it was clear that from the preceding evening of -- the evening preceding the attack, there had been military preparations. And assuming that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were still not implied [sic] at that stage, what was going around their houses on the 16th of April was something they simply could not not know. And knowing what was happening, they could not not understand what that meant. The third element, as was admitted by the accused when they testified, in the morning that day they did nothing to warn, to forewarn their neighbours. And given the information that allegedly was given to them, the only thing they could do is think that, like them, the Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici were at risk. During cross-examination, Zoran Kupreskic was very clear in admitting that. I quote him: "I had all reasons to believe that these people were coming from outside, that the Mujahedins were coming from outside, and they were going to wreak havoc among my Muslim neighbours. I didn't know that army. I didn't know those soldiers. We heard that they were killing people, cutting throats of people, that they were burning houses. It may be that the Muslims were afraid of them too. We were afraid of the Vitezovi, of the Zuti of the TPN. The Muslims were afraid of them too. We were trying to get away from them, not be close to them. Therefore, I could think that the Muslims would also try to get away from the village and did not expect the Mujahedins to arrive." And this failure to act by Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic in those circumstances could only be an advantage to the attackers, could only promote the success in their endeavour. The fourth element the Prosecution are basing their arguments on is, of course, the statement by Witness C. Witness C, and you will remember, Your Honours, was then a very young boy. He was 13 1/2. He was evicted from his house after his brother was killed in front of him and he was taken to Jozo Alilovic's house. He was hidden in a house very close to that of Jozo Alilovic, together with Tomislav, Jozo's brother. Towards late morning he saw four men in camouflage uniforms arrive. They had green shoulder ribbons. And he recognised among them men Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Dragan Papic's brother and Ako. You will remember this man testified here in Court. In Court the witnesses mixed up Zoran and Mirjan, confused them. But to me this should not challenge the witness's credibility, since the latter pointed collectively at Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic; he clearly identified them without a single hesitation. Did the witness make a mistake or did he lie? There is little reason to believe that he made a mistake. He knew the accused perfectly well. He saw them at close range and always he was very accurate in the way he told the events that he experienced. Could he have lied? I would say that, as a rule, when a witness lies, he fails to mention third parties who could come testify to say the opposite. And I think that if, through a lie, Witness C wanted to harm the brothers, the Kupreskic brothers, he would not have mentioned other people than those two Kupreskic brothers. Also, if you want to lie, you need to have a reason for it, and the reason was not ascertained in Court. There was no single trace of any motivation that would have prompted him to lie. I would like now to come to the attack on the house of Witness H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
