utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, everything is settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I had reached the point when there was this attack on the house of Witness H. You will remember, Your Honours, Witness H, in April 1993, was 13 years old. She lived in a house close to the Kupreskic houses; she lived there, together with her father, her mother, and her two younger sisters. During the trial, we saw photographs of the house, and you will remember the somewhat unusual layout of the house. There is a kind of cellar, which can be accessed through a trapdoor which is in the children's room, and there is another opening out onto the garage. In December 1993, this witness spoke to the examining magistrate in Zenica, and also later in 1998, she told this Tribunal what had happened on that day, on the 16th of April, in the house. When the family heard the first shots, the parents came to wake up the daughters. They all went down into the cellar through that trapdoor. Grenades were being thrown into the house. Outside of the house, in front of the garage door, the father was called by his first name and he was told he had to open the door. Witness H believed that those voices were friendly voices, the voices of people who wanted to join them in the shelter, and she told her father that she opened the garage door. She couldn't believe that those people, the attackers, would use the first name of her father to call him. The father left the cellar, opened the garage door, and then the witness heard that her father was told to come out. The father was begging for something and then shots of automatic rifle were heard. The trapdoor was open above her, the one leading to the children's room. She heard a male voice asking who was down there. She said that her mother was in a state of shock, unable to utter a word, holding tightly her two little daughters. The witness left the cellar and found herself facing Zoran Kupreskic. He's facing her, only a metre away from her, no more, and she recognised him beyond any reasonable doubt. He was in a uniform, had black paint over his face, and was holding an automatic rifle. She told him that her mother and her sisters were downstairs. He asked whether there were weapons down in the cellar, whether the men were hiding in the cellar, because he said that he had been ordered to kill them all. Then, according to the witness's testimony, Zoran went away a few steps to get closer to Mirjan, who was wearing the same uniform and the same equipment as his brother. Zoran asked Mirjan what he was to do with them; Mirjan said he didn't know. Then Zoran went back towards the witness and ordered everybody to leave the cellar. The witness knelt down in front of Zoran, begging him to spare their lives. There was Mirjan and Zoran, but according to the witness, there were three other soldiers in the house too, in the kitchen, one in front of the front door, and they were trying to torch the house with petrol. Now, what do we think of this testimony? First of all, there is no confusion or error possible when it comes to Witness H. She says she recognised a man whom she knew very well. They were only a few metres from her; they spoke to her. So not only did she recognise their look, she also recognised their voices. Witness H cannot have made a mistake, but could she have lied? Could it be that, among witnesses, some arrangement has been made, according to which, as has been suggested by the Defence, or as has been suggested by the accused during their testimony, was there an arrangement, a pact concluded among various witnesses who think that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic should be held responsible for the Croats? In order to refute such an argument, I will call your attention to various elements. They are as follows: First, on the 17th of December, 1993, Witness H was heard by the examining magistrate in Zenica. I'm trying to think of this hearing, and I refer to the testimony of Mrs. Ajanovic, the examining magistrate. There is no doubt left, even though the witness seems to have forgotten about such a meeting. As to the essential, the striking feature when you look at the written statement of the 17th of December, 1993, which is Defence Exhibit 1-2, on all the major points, as to the fact that the attackers knew of the cellar, knew that Zoran and Mirjan spoke to her, that they spoke among each other, that the witness had to kneel down in front of one of them; the fact that she, together with her mother, were driven away from the house by these people, by the aggressors; on all these major points, the testimony here in this Tribunal, and that made in front of the magistrate in Zenica, go in the same direction. As soon as December 1993, we see the name of the accused, Zoran and Mirjan, in a statement taken by an examining magistrate, and this is a major point to be taken into account. I shall, however, notice -- and this may be some kind of concession made to the Defence -- like Witness C, Witness H seems to confuse, to mix up Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, and upon a closer reading of her statement of December 1993, it looks as though it was Mirjan, and not Zoran, who opened the trapdoor, and that it was Zoran who was somewhat behind. But this does not impinge at all on the witness's credibility as to the essential things this witness told us. She knew the accused and she may have been mixed up as to the first names. The second point: The written statements of the mother of Witness H. The Prosecution wanted to call Witness H's mother, but this person was not able to testify in court in view of her state of health. The Court heard the head of the Victims and Witnesses Unit, who conveyed the opinion of the doctor, and a medical certificate was produced. The written statement of the mother was tendered into evidence. It is very important, in my view, to note that on the 23rd of April, 1993, in a written statement, the mother of Witness H said that her daughter told her that she had recognised Zoran Kupreskic in the house. It is true, and again I can see that to the Defence, that the mother of Witness H later made statements which are broadly inconsistent. But according to us, the description given of Witness H of her mother, a mother totally overcome by anguish and panic, incapable of speaking, that can explain the inconsistency of the new statement. But it is important to remember that the mother, Witness H, reported what her daughter had said, which this witness then developed before the investigating judge and later in this Court. From the house of Witness H, I should like us now to go on to the house of Witness KL. These two houses are very close, one to another. There are some ten metres between them. And there is a technical link between them, which was revealed by experts of the Dutch police. The Court will remember that in front of the house of Witness H, a cartridge was discovered, and it appears to be probable, as said by Witness Kerkhoff, that this cartridge discovered in front of the house of Witness H, and three other cartridges found in the house of Witness KL, come from the same weapon. Regarding what happened in the house of Witness KL, the Court will remember the very long testimony by this witness. He said that in April '93 he lived in that house with his son, daughter-in-law, a child of six or seven, who was the son of his daughter-in-law, and a three-month-old baby, his grandson. The witness had a room adjacent to the main room in the house of his family. On the 16th of April at 5.30, a few seconds after the first explosions, soldiers entered the house. This soldier, who the witness recognised when he entered the main room from his room as Zoran Kupreskic. Behind him came Mirjan Kupreskic. The light was on in the room and this allowed him to recognise these two people. Zoran Kupreskic, according to the witness, immediately shot the son of the witness, and then he shot the daughter-in-law, and then he went towards the young boy lying on the sofa. At the same time Mirjan poured some liquid from a bottle and set it on fire. Witness KL was forced to the ground, his head hit against the wall, and he loses consciousness for a few short minutes. Zoran, according to the witness, shoots in his direction, without hitting him, because the bullets are in the armrest. Then the baby cries out. There is a new burst of fire. Finally, the attackers withdraw. According to the witness, Zoran had black paint on his face and both of them were dressed in black uniforms. That was the testimony of this witness in Court. This witness had, of course, before appearing in Court, made a large number of statements. I shall refer to the three first ones. He first made a statement on the 22nd of April, 1993 before a representative of a research institute for crimes against humanity, and he did not name Zoran or Mirjan. Then a statement on the 1st of October, 1993, before an investigating judge in Zenica, and he said that he did not recognise the face of the attackers, but that they resembled Zoran and Mirjan. A third declaration on the 20th of February, 1994, before a representative of the same research institute, in which he names Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic as the two Ustashes who massacred his family and destroyed his house. Witness KL, while he was in hospital, also made a statement in the form of a television interview, which was broadcast in April 1993. I will admit to the Defence that if we look in detail at these statements and those made to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, there are numerous contradictions. But in my view, it is important to note that he did not name the attackers before the 20th of February, 1994. Why? The question was put to him by yourself, Mr. President, in Court. And he explained that he did not have the courage to do so because the war was on and nobody knew how it would end, and that later on he came to the conclusion that he should not protect the authors -- the perpetrators of the massacre. These contradictions between the statements of the witness and the delay of the witness naming the attackers, should this lead us to believe that he was interfered with, or that he deliberately testified against innocents? Regarding the credibility of Witness KL, I shall make some general statements first. The Court knows well that the written statement of a witness is the result of an exercise of two people: the witness and the investigator for the statement. To be exact and complete, the investigator has to have talent and experience, but we don't know anything of the -- about the professional qualities of those who took the first statements from the Witness KL. Also, I should like to underline that the moral qualities of the witness were fine-combed, and nothing was found. A few incidents referred to by the Defence are so rare and so old that one can say that he has absolutely passed the test of morality. This is an important element to be borne in mind. He had no reason to bear a grudge against the accused. And if the witness lied, he had no motive to explain his lies. I should also like to underline that evidence has proven that Witness KL was a witness of the assassination of his family. The recounting of the facts was made from the first hearings; two men, one shooting the other, setting the house on fire. There are contradictions, but they seem to me to be of secondary importance. We have his story, which was confirmed by technical investigations carried out by Dutch police officers. These investigations were partial, but nevertheless important. Witness Prudon, the Dutch police officer who examined the house in July 1998, in spite of the limited time at his disposal, made some discoveries, and none of them contradict the story of Witness KL. The bones of the baby, for instance, discovered in the house, were burnt, according to this expert, at a very high temperature of 1.000 to 1.630 degrees Celsius. At this very high temperature, the explanation could be that the attacker used a combustion accelerator. No traces of that were found, that is true, but Witness van der Peyl, an expert, a chemical expert attached to the justice ministry of the Netherlands, said that it was possible, in view of the time that has passed and the condition of the house, that those traces simply disappeared in the course of the period of time that had passed. In the part of the room where Witness KL said he saw Mirjan Kupreskic pour an inflammable liquid, the wooden floor itself burnt, which could mean, according to Witness Prudon, a concentration of fire in those places, a hotbed of fire. According to the story of Witness KL, there are a certain number of strange points, and I myself said when I learnt about it that I was astonished by some of those points. But regarding most of those points, Witness KL gave explanations which are quite convincing. For example, I was astonished that in his first statement the witness did not mention that he was behind a sofa, but in the statement of Witness KL taken on the 5th of May 1993 by a representative of the Commission of the Rights of Man, it is said that the witness hid behind a sofa. So it is quite clear that a certain number of contradictions can be attributed to the way in which those statements were taken. Also, another example, I could not understand that he could escape death by disappearing behind the armrest of the sofa, feeling the cartridges hit his legs as they were ejected from an automatic rifle. But we know that these bullets came from an AK-47, which have trajectory towards the right and forward, as shown by Witness Kerkhoff. As for the question of identification now, I should like to underline first of all that Witness KL never gave a different name than those of the accused, though it is true that he took some time to name them. It has not been proven, it seems to me, that Witness KL had publicly during his televised interview in April 1993 said that he did not know the assassins of his family. The two witnesses that we heard in this connection do not seem to me to have been sufficiently convincing, in view of the highly selective nature of their memories. I wish also to underline that the delay in naming the attackers was only formal because, in reality, very soon, and even before the end of the month of April, the name of Kupreskic appeared in connection with the massacre of the family of Witness KL. And the source can obviously be no other than the witness, the only surviving person of that massacre. In fact, as early as the end of May 1993, the notion appears that the perpetrators of the crime were neighbours. A witness was present in Zenica for an international convention and who speaks the Bosnian language, met Witness KL at Zenica hospital on the 7th of May, and he told him that he knew the names of the murderers. He said that they were neighbours from the first house. In addition, Witness JJ told the Tribunal that she had heard on the radio a few days before the 16th of April that the crimes in Ahmici had been committed by several individuals who were named. The name of Zoran Kupreskic was mentioned. The witness said somewhat later, on the 24th or 25th of April, during a meeting with the witness, that Zoran himself mentioned the name of the Witness KL. He said that he was accused by that family of having killed one of them, and of course he denied his guilt, but the fact in and of itself is important. When he testified, Witness JJ asserted that he could not have made any mistakes or not have confused anything in respect of the moment when he received the confidences from Zoran Kupreskic. Very quickly and unofficially, but in a certain way, Witness KL names at least Zoran Kupreskic. Could he have made an error in good faith? The answer, obviously, is no, because he knew both people that he identified very well and for a long time; they were people he knew very well. The distance separating them was very small and there was enough light, and those two individuals did not really try to hide, probably thinking that they would leave no living witnesses behind. There is a final possibility which was raised by the Defence; that is, with the other witnesses who had accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, had they set up kind of a false agreement not to tell the truth? The Tribunal, of course, will have its own opinion on that issue, but I would like to make two comments. The first is that it's very difficult to believe that this type of pact could have been arranged in the days that followed the massacre, given the situation of the victims at that time. My second comment is that it seems to me that in that assertion, there is a serious contradiction which affects the Defence. We're told both that Zoran and Mirjan were modest individuals who played only an insignificant role and that people wanted to turn them into scapegoats for Croatian guilt. I believe that if the witnesses had tried to find a scapegoat, that is, an emblematic form of guilty, they could have found other people, perhaps people who were more influential and more well-known than the two accused. Lastly, I believe that we can understand, without too much difficulty, Witness KL and the belated amount of time he took in naming the attackers of his family. It is not easy for that witness, who is also the victim of a very serious crime, to state the names of witnesses as perpetrators of those crimes. We know that within the weeks and even the first months following the massacre at Ahmici, the situation in the Lasva Valley was very uncertain and the result of the conflict was not something one could foresee. The simple carrying out of justice at that time was, in fact, improbable, even though officially a resolution had been taken in order to set up this Tribunal. The victims are isolated, without support and without any resources, and probably those victims, or at least some of them, could not break with Ahmici, even if they had been driven out. They could not break with their homes, even if their homes were lying in ruins, and some of the victims must have had difficulty imagining a life anywhere else than Ahmici. Citing the name of a Croatian neighbour as the perpetrator of a crime would be burning all the bridges behind one, that is, cutting off any hope of returning to Ahmici, and we can understand that to mention the Kupreskics as having been near the burning houses is not the same thing as designating the murderers of one's family. I mentioned several Defence arguments. I would like to mention two others. The Defence said, and will continue to say, that the accused are incapable of having acted as the Prosecution claims, given their human qualities. I will not go into a discussion in this trial of the human qualities of the accused, but I must say that on the morning of the 16th of April, according to what they themselves said, whereas they had the time and the opportunity to flee, they did not take any steps to warn their Muslim friends or neighbours about a situation in which the Muslims themselves could not be completely safe. As regards the assistance given by Zoran to his friend, Witness JJ, I would not like to challenge that, but I do wonder that in the name of what was that assistance given to Witness JJ. I would say that it was not in the name of humanity, but rather that it was in the name of a friendship, a friendship which was close and exclusive, and that from that interest, Witness JJ apparently was the only one who enjoyed that assistance. The Defence also invokes a type of alibi; that is, that there was a time spent in a declivity behind the houses, that they tried to see what was going on, although they couldn't from that viewpoint. We heard a great many witnesses who agreed on the same story. All the witnesses, or at least most of them, mentioned the 30 military policemen, or about 30 policemen, they described them all in the same way, and those military police provoked among all the victims the same feelings of anguish and repulsion. All of the witnesses mentioned the three days that they spent in the depression without being able practically to move and without knowing anything about what was going on, without knowing, for instance, what houses were burning. We have difficulty in believing that that actually occurred, when we know that a depression could not be a shelter for the accused and for their friends, could not be a way of guaranteeing the safety of their families; when we know that as early as the end of the morning, at the latest, Zoran and Mirjan were in contact with Nikola Omazic, whom we know was a member of the HVO that was implicated in the attack; whereas we know that as early as the middle of the day of the 16th of April, Vlatko Kupreskic said that he was able to move about without any problems between Zume and his house; when we know that other individuals, during that same morning, were moving about freely in order to tell the accused that Fahrudin Ahmic had died. In the same way, Drago Josipovic is described to us as coming and going in the middle of the battlefield in Ahmici. And when we know or when we remember that Zoran told us that on the morning of the 16th of April, he had heard women, who he recognised as being Muslims, screaming with terror. And lastly, we know that the purpose of the attack on the civilian population of Ahmici had reached its target, at the latest, at the end of the afternoon of the 16th of April, with the destruction of the minaret. I will not mention all the details about which the witnesses agreed, after so much time has gone by since the facts occurred, but it is clear to me, I think, that even faced with only the allegations of the Defence I just mentioned, that that alibi loses its credibility. Obviously, we are struck at the stories told by the witnesses of what happened on the 16th of April, 1993, including what happened also -- also what happened on the 20th of October, 1992, whereas the circumstances were obviously completely different, and everything collapses even further when we listen to Witness JJ. Witness JJ said that Zoran, as early as the 16th of April, called his home in order to ask him to look for a shelter. Witness JJ said that Zoran Kupreskic had told him a little bit later, around the 21st of April, that before the first shooting during the night of the 15th to the 16th of April, with his car, he had taken several trips and he had brought his whole family to safety in Ravno. The same Witness JJ said that on the 16th of April, the members of the Jokers unit were firing on the fleeing civilians, that one of the Jokers noticed that Zoran was not firing and then threatened him with a weapon if he did not decide finally to fire. Then, in order to save himself, he fired in the air, not on the civilian; he fired in the air. Why did he do that and why did he say that to his friend, Witness JJ? If he said that, then the Judges will have to decide whether this is true and whether he lied to the Witness JJ. If he told the truth, then he lied to the Tribunal. In light of everything that we know after the trial, it is clear, I believe, that for the Prosecution, Zoran Kupreskic did not tell the truth, either to his friend, Witness JJ, or to the Judges. Both to his friend and to the Judges, Zoran Kupreskic had good reasons to hide the truth. In light of all of these elements that were heard during the proceedings, and of course during the time that I have, I can only briefly mention them, and I will ask the Tribunal's Judges to say that Counts 1 to 11 against accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were established by the evidence and that all the evidence to be considered, submitted to the Tribunal during this trial, must be evaluated. Now I will go to the situation of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. Against the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, the Prosecution considers that it proved that he personally participated in the attack of the HVO against the civilian Muslim population of Ahmici and that through his behaviour and his acts, he facilitated the achievement of that attack and its success. The Prosecution submits that it established in the same way that he was personally and directly responsible with other people for the death of Fata Pezer and for the wounding of her daughter, Dzenana Pezer. I would first like to mention the question that many witnesses of the Defence raised, that is, the medical condition of the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic. It is not being challenged by the Prosecution that Vlatko Kupreskic, when he was a child, may have had serious health problems, and it is undoubtedly true that the accused, in 1970, it was said that he was unfit for military service. It has been established that in May of 1993, there was an examining commission for the HVO, and the HVO said that he was not suitable for military service. But before May, what was the situation? The idea of service in peacetime within the former Yugoslavia certainly is different from service in wartimes for the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia, under the circumstances of 1992 and 1993, and one could not believe that the ordinary citizen that Vlatko Kupreskic claims to have been could have put forth, against the order of mobilisation in April, the fact that he was judged to be unfit for service in 1970 by the authorities of the former Yugoslavia. The decision that he not go to the army of 27 May 1993, that is, Exhibit D16/3, was presented not only to the accused but also to the Vitez Brigade, and it's the proof that Vlatko Kupreskic was now part of that brigade, and this is what confirms document 30/35, which is a report on the mobilisation, in which it appears that the accused was deployed into the HVO active forces during the period starting on the 16th of April, 1993. But it may be that this entire discussion as to whether Vlatko Kupreskic was a member of the HVO loses its relevance, is irrelevant, because it appeared, through the testimony heard in court, that at the relevant times, the accused was in no way handicapped, limited in his movement, in his activities. More often than not, he's described as being a very active and dynamic person, especially conducting business. Later, when he was arrested, he used an AK-47, which was a weapon he kept loaded and ready to be fired. The Defence witness, Mario Rajic, testified on the 8th of February, 1999 and said that if you want to use an AK-47, you need to be trained. Therefore, the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic, was, physically speaking, perfectly able to carry out the part ascribed to him by the Prosecution. Another factor to be considered by this Court is the nationalistic involvement of Vlatko Kupreskic, which is beyond any doubt. This is what prompted him to claim that he was part of the HVO. I refer here to document 329, which is the certificate showing that Vlatko Kupreskic was a member of the Vitez Brigade in the period from the 16th of April, 1993 to the 15th of January, 1996. We have heard other testimony. I referred to Witness T, who stated that during October '92 she saw Vlatko Kupreskic, together with his wife and another man, taking weapons out of a car and taking those weapons into his house. I also recall the testimony of Witness H, who reported an event that took place much later than the 16th of April, '93. When she returned to have a look at her house, she met Vlatko Kupreskic, who asked her what she was doing there, who told her that it was no longer her house, that her house would never be hers anymore. I am aware that during his testimony, the accused in his Defence insisted at length on the fact that Vlatko Kupreskic was a businessman conducting business with members of all communities; that he had business transactions with Croatia. I would like to state generally that while business does not necessarily mean neutrality, is not tantamount to neutrality, because it can't be carried out freely in time of war. On the contrary, it implies close links with the authorities, and the ruling authority at the time is the HVO. Indeed, looking at Exhibits 359, 377 and 378, you see that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic turns out to be much more involved than he claims to have been with the HVO authorities. Exhibit 359, as you recall, is an inventory established by a commission. It is dated February '93 and signed, among other signatories, by Vlatko. His signature was authenticated here in Court by his wife and the document was not challenged at all. Document 377 is a report dated 28th of December, '92, addressed to the interior minister, as to the forces of the Vitez police forces. And Vlatko Kupreskic is mentioned therein as a first-class inspector in charge of, I quote, "fighting offences of special interest for the state." Document 378 is dated the 22nd of February, '93. It is an inspection report of the Vitez police, mentioning the accused as a officer in charge of fighting criminality, and no doubt with a special mission for the state, on behalf of the state. During cross-examination the accused explained that this was just an administrative arrangement aimed at paying him for the work he had done. I regard his justification as particularly inconsistent, all the more so since you know that he carried out this inventory in a commission that was made up only of police members and that the final report is no longer than three pages. Obviously, these documents show that he enjoyed the collaboration of the official HVO authorities. These documents also show that at a given point in time and for a specific period of time, Vlatko Kupreskic was a member of both a civilian and special police force, which could account for the fact that he is not to be found among the army before April 1993. But in my view, this also raises the question of today, of what is still hidden or unknown today as to the part played by the accused Vlatko Kupreskic at the time in the Vitez area. Third observation. It is in connection with the alleged trip to Croatia on the eve and two days before the 16th of April, 1993. I shall not dwell very long on this because eventually the accused acknowledged that he was present in Ahmici as of the late afternoon of the 15th of April. However, I want to stress the fact that according to me, we did not receive the evidence beyond any reasonable doubt of that trip. We have received no document by way of evidence, no document showing that business dealings had been concluded which could have attested of the trip factually taking place. The Court will remember that many Prosecution witnesses met Vlatko Kupreskic prior to the 16th of April attack, during the preceding days, in the Vitez area and in Ahmici, at a time when the accused claims that he was away on a trip. I refer specially to Witness B, who saw Vlatko Kupreskic on several occasions from October '92 to April 1993 in the Vitez hotel. He saw him on the last time on the 15th of April in the afternoon of that day. I also refer to Witness L, who lives along the road close to Vlatko Kupreskic's house. Witness L explained that he was coming back from Zume on foot on the 15th of April. It was about 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. On his way home he passed in front of the Sutre store and Vlatko Kupreskic's house, in front of the store. He saw Vlatko Kupreskic together with other people, some 10 people whom he didn't know. At the balcony of Vlatko Kupreskic's house he saw soldiers. Witness M saw, before dusk, on the 15th of April, a truck stopping in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house; soldiers got off and entered his house. Witness M's statement is corroborated by Witness O, who saw, in the afternoon of the 15th of April, four to six soldiers enter the yard of Vlatko Kupreskic's house. Therefore, it is impossible for us to believe that Vlatko Kupreskic may have returned from a business trip to Croatia in the evening of the 15th of April knowing nothing of what was afoot. We have to observe that his house and the immediate surroundings were used for war preparations. And even if the accused had not been otherwise informed, he could not but have noticed that there were war preparations, he could not but have understood the meaning thereof. I'd like also to show that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic could not have ignored that the attackers used this house in the offences directed by the HVO forces against the civilian population at Ahmici. It has been demonstrated through several pieces of testimony that his house and its immediate surroundings were used as of the very beginning of the attack and throughout the day by the HVO forces. His house was a base for action carried out against the Muslim houses and their surroundings. It was also used in order to close that trap organised against those Muslim trying to escape towards Upper Ahmici. We do remember that as of the very first minutes of the attack, some neighbouring houses were attacked. We remember that the first civilians trying to escape, to flee towards Upper Ahmici, were stopped in front of the accused's house in front of the Sutre store. We do remember that during the morning of the 16th of April, many women were especially targeted, were killed or wounded in front of his house. Witness W was trapped lower down from his house, was forced to stay there for three or four hours, and his wife is then hit in the head by a bullet and she didn't survive. Witness X was too trapped in front of that house, from 8.00 in the morning until noon. One of her daughters was killed, another wounded, after her husband had been shot in front of her very eyes on another location at close range. In front of that house Witness X saw Slavko Sakic, son of Niko Sakic, a resident of Ahmici, who was together with the soldiers. Witness WB confirmed that his house was a trap, where all those trying to escape from Ahmici were caught, and that many soldiers were there gathered in front of his house. Witness WB told us that in the beginning of the afternoon those soldiers could be heard congratulating themselves for the good work done. Major Dooley observed that around 1.30 on that day, operations were launched with large-calibre guns, with 50-calibre, from his house. Witness N too saw a large-calibre weapon positioned in front of the Sutre store. The accused alleged that his house was used without his knowing it, and that he found it looted and damaged by the soldiers. This allegation has not in any way been proven in the course of the proceedings. A document dated 5 April '95 shows that some damage was caused to the house, but we also know that that same house was burglarised on the 7th of May, 1994, and that on that occasion some damage was caused to the front door and the balcony. The accused said that he had to leave his house, which was uninhabitable after the 16th of April, and that he lived after that as a refugee. However, several days after the aggression, Corporal Skillen, who was walking through the village, was surprised to see on the balcony of Vlatko Kupreskic's house a woman and a child sitting there which, and I quote the witness, "appeared to be living a perfectly normal day and behaving as if nothing had happened in the village of Ahmici." A little while later, passing in front of that same home, Corporal Skillen noticed two adults in uniform who had joined that woman and child on the balcony. Witness G, hidden in a house not far from the lower mosque, about three days after the massacre saw Vlatko Kupreskic getting out of his car and entering a house that had belonged to a Muslim. I should also like to underline that several witnesses reported the closeness between Franjo Kupreskic, the father of Vlatko, and the soldiers. Witness W said that after his wife had been hit by a bullet below Vlatko's house early in the afternoon, he addressed Franjo, asking him for a wheelbarrow to transport his wife, or an instrument to be able to make a stretcher. Franjo refused, but a soldier asked him to agree, and Franjo gave him an axe with which he could cut branches to make a stretcher. The testimony of Witness X, which at the beginning of the afternoon decided to surrender, if we can use that word, to the soldiers accompanying her. And she saw Franjo Kupreskic accompanied by HVO soldiers, who was not threatened but, on the contrary, quite at his ease. In fact, he was, if not in a position of command, then he had a position of influence over the soldiers who were deployed around that house. Consequently, in view of all these elements and the ease of the father of the accused, we cannot believe that the house was used without the accused knowing it. We also have to confirm this, the testimony of two witnesses, Witness H and Witness KL, according to which, at the beginning of the morning, around 6.00 on the 16th of April, the accused Vlatko Kupreskic was close to his house. I come now to the testimony of Witness Q, who was the main witness for the specific crime the accused is charged with. Witness Q was living with Fata, his wife, three of his children, his daughter-in-law, and three children of his daughter-in-law. Between 5.20 and 5.30 that morning, when he was getting ready to go to work, the shooting started. He rallied together his family, as well as the family of his brother, and other refugees joined them. He left his house and went to a pantry, where they spent some time. Later, around 8.00 or 8.30, forming a group of 14, roughly 14 persons, forming a column, they walked towards Upper Ahmici. All these people were in civilian clothes. None of them had any weapons. Witness Q was at the tail end of the column. We have seen photographs and films of the place where these events took place. We know that the path follows a narrow valley, that to the left there is a long hill that separates the road from the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, and on the right there is another hill parallel with the first, but higher and longer. Going upwards, these people were for a moment exposed to the soldiers positioned in and around the house of Vlatko Kupreskic. The group was trying to climb the hill to the right, to move away from the road where the danger was. When they reached the top of the hill, they heard insults. Witness Q turned around and saw four men close to Vlatko Kupreskic's house, three soldiers in camouflage uniform who he cannot identify, and the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in civilian clothing. All were armed. Vlatko was carrying his weapon to the ready. After the cries, these men, the four men, including the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, opened fire at the group and the people who were fleeing. First of all, the daughter of the witness is wounded. She called her mother. Her mother retraced her steps. Her mother is hit; in the same way and virtually at the same time, one of the refugees who was a member of this fleeing group. At this moment Witness Q drags his daughter towards the opposite side of the hill to shelter her from the shooting coming from Vlatko's house. Then he comes back for his wife and drags her too to the place where he had left his daughter. Numerous witnesses and documents have been used by the Defence to challenge the place indicated by Witness Q as being the place where his wife was killed and his daughter wounded. In an effort to establish that at the moment of shooting, the group could not be seen from the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, the Defence relied on the statements of Witness CF to a large extent. We know that this Witness CF, who was a refugee, did not know the topography of the area, and the indications he gave five years later about it obviously lack credibility. We were able to note that the tail of Witness Q regarding the path covered by the group and the position of his wife and daughter, when the wife was killed and the daughter wounded, were corroborated by Witnesses P, R, S and T. These witnesses told us that when they left to flee towards Upper Ahmici, firing from high-calibre weapons came from the south, that is, from the main road, and the hill was exposed to risk, and that is why the other path at that moment appeared to be safer. Furthermore, all the witnesses said that they stopped at the food pantry, which is a building dug into the hill, closed by a door, at 35 or 40 metres from the house of Witness Q, according to the statements given by Howard Tucker, an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor. Leaving this place, they turned right towards Upper Ahmici and not left, to retrace their steps and go towards the house of Witness Q. Even for the Defence, Witness CE, the wife of Witness CF, confirmed this. Finally, Witness CF himself, when appearing in the Tribunal, did not have precise memories. According to a statement in 1998, they were shot at from the direction of the Sutre store. Is it a mistake regarding the place where the people were killed and wounded, members of the family of Witness Q? However, this was corroborated by the discovery on the top of the hill of personal belongings that Witness Q and Witness R recognised as belonging to members of their family. The Defence also challenged that Witness Q, in view of the distance between him and the firing soldiers, could have recognised the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic. One can remember that Professor Wagenaar appeared on behalf of the Defence at the Tribunal, who said that the identification of people at a distance of 60 metres, though possible, has a significant risk of error of the order of 50 per cent. We can recall that the distance separating the accused from the witness, according to the statements of the witness, was assessed to be 53 metres. However, it seems to me that the experiments on which Professor Wagenaar relies are not relevant, in view of the specific situation, because, according to his protocol, it was a question of recognising a particular face from a photograph among different photographs, and we have to note that this experimental plan could not take into account, first of all, the noteworthy difference that exists between recognising a face on a photograph and a person in reality, in relief and in colour, the size, the behaviour, the movement, the gestures. Secondly, it does not take into account the fact that the witness knew perfectly and for a long time the person that he says he identified and that he had seen him often. The distance certainly is an important factor, but we have not heard from the expert in which circumstances it can be considered important. The work of Professor Wagenaar is not of great assistance to us, that is true, but we know from personal experience that it is easy for us to recognise somebody whom we know well by his stature, his morphology, and his visual features, even if we see him at a great distance. I should like to add that the testimony was partially corroborated by Witness S, who saw a group of three soldiers and a civilian, and also that Witness Q proved his credibility because there was no inconsistency in his overall testimony. The accused Vlatko Kupreskic presented an alibi in court, and we heard several witnesses, among them his wife, to confirm this alibi; however, without entering into the details of the inconsistency and uncertainty that exist, I should like very briefly to say why we cannot believe his story. First of all, there is an important discord between the statement made on the 11th of June, 1998 and the testimony in court, especially regarding the time when he reached his house and the presence of soldiers in or around his house. Also, very grave inconsistencies emerge regarding the reason why he left his shelter and went to his house. He said, in the course of his testimony, that he was worried about his father, whom he had to leave alone because of his health, and in a written letter to the Prosecutor in November 1997, the wife of the accused said that her husband had received an order to go to the house of Niko Sakic, where he had to care for the wounded. According to the testimony heard by this Court from the accused and Niko Sakic, it is, indeed, in the house of the latter that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic went after leaving the shelter. Consequently, his concern for his father at the time was not so great, as we know from other witnesses of the Prosecution that the father of the accused was not, under any circumstances, in any danger, and his health would have allowed him, without any doubt, to get to the shelter, as he did in fact in the afternoon. Apparently, the accused received orders to take care of the wounded, and we have a last question here, and that is why the accused did not appear when the body of Mirjan Santic, for instance, was transported towards Zume or when Nikola Omazic was wounded, because neither Zoran Kupreskic, nor his brother Mirjan, nor any other people accompanying them, did see during that day the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. So that it seems to me, in view of all these inconsistencies, that we have very little idea as to the real role played by the accused Vlatko Kupreskic in the course of that day, and everything seems to indicate that he was very closely associated with the HVO attack and, in any event, present in front of his house when shootings were made and when some people were killed and wounded. In view of all these factors and evidence collected by the Prosecution, which I have referred to briefly, I ask the Court to find the accused guilty of Counts 1, 12 to 15.
