utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I now move to the charges against the accused Dragan Papic. I believe the Prosecutor has established that he personally participated and actively participated in the persecution of the civilian Muslim population of Ahmici on the 16th of April. Firstly, I would refer to his nationalistic commitments, and I would refer to all of the Prosecution witnesses, and there are many of them, who unanimously stated that before April 1993, they would frequently see Dragan Papic wearing a black uniform and with a rifle. All the witnesses also said that Dragan Papic's behaviour toward them, that is, towards the Muslims, was clearly threatening and intimidating. Secondly, I refer to document 371, which is the register of the HDZ for the period September 1991 to April 1992. The name of the accused as a member of the HDZ party appears, as well as his signature. I would also like to bring out that the accused, Dragan Papic, at that time was an active member of a military unit of the HVO. I would refer to several people who testified, specifically to the testimony received by the Defence. For the Defence, the witness Zvonimir Santic stated that on the 20th of October, 1992, at around 8.00 in the morning, he saw Dragan Papic with an M-60 mortar and a bag, and he said that he received the order to go to Njive from Nenad Santic. This was corroborated by the accused's defence during the opening remarks. It, therefore, appears that on the 20th of October, 1992, the accused was executing military-type orders and using a war weapon, because, of course, the use of a mortar is a prerogative for the military and not a civilian occupation. Witness B mentions a roadblock that was set up in front of Ahmici, in front of Papic's house, in November of 1992, and on the roadblock, you could see sandbags and a machine gun. The witness met Nenad Santic, Mario Cerkez, and Dragan Papic there, and during those negotiations, Dragan Papic gave them the command to dismantle the roadblock. Therefore, he is the one who is in command, according to the statement of Witness B. Before the 16th of April, 1993, Dragan Papic's house was frequently used as a base by the armed HVO forces. It was still used in October 1992 because, according to the witnesses, and specifically I'm referring to Witness D and to Witness Mehmed Ahmic, shots could be seen coming from that house, and Mehmed said that he himself had been the target of fire by an automatic weapon. In January 1993, the witness Fahrudin Ahmic saw the accused, accompanied with other people, carrying military materiel outside the house. Witness B, after October 1992, saw heavy weaponry placed around Dragan Papic's house. So the house was frequently used as a centre for military activity. Other elements put forth by the Prosecution, sometimes also by the Defence, establish the fact that the accused belonged to a military unit, and I'm referring to document D18/2, which is dated February 1993, in which the accused appears as part of the personnel of the 2nd Vitez Brigade. Dragan Papic's name appears there, with the detail that he was brought into the army on the 23rd of June, 1992. On the 16th of April, 1993, the accused's house was used, as it was in October 1992, as a fire base, as a support base, by the Croatian forces. Several witnesses stated that significant military activity was deployed on the 16th of April, 1993 around that house. I am referring to the witness Fahrudin Ahmic, who testified for the Prosecution, as well as Witness A, who saw a machine gun on the 16th of April, 1993 near Dragan Papic's house. Dragan Papic was in the village on the 16th of April, 1993, and he participated in the attack against the civilian Muslim population. Witness G stated that during the morning of the 16th of April, on the threshold of Ahmet Husein's house, Ahmet Husein's body was lying on the ground and that at about 10 metres from him, he saw Dragan Papic standing. Dragan Papic was wearing a uniform and carrying a rifle. Other soldiers were near him, and the witness would see Dragan Papic during the afternoon together with other soldiers. This testimony appeared to be credible in light of the fact that Witness G was very familiar with Dragan Papic, since for a long time he had been a close neighbour. And as regards his entire statement, the witness did not contradict himself at all or demonstrate any inconsistency in his testimony. Witness A saw Dragan Papic on the next day, that is, the 17th of April, again wearing a uniform, in front of his house, next to a machine-gun, together with other soldiers. And according to Witness A, the accused made jokes at the expense of the Muslim refugees who were being taken to a detention centre. I would now tell you -- say that the Defence stated through that witness, not through Dragan Papic, who chose not to speak, that the accused was ignorant of what was being planned there on the 16th of April, and that throughout that day of 16th April he was not in Ahmici but rather on the Radak Bridge, where he was responsible for holding the guard. First, in order to respond to that thesis of the Defence, I would like to say that in giving the closeness of the links between Dragan Papic and the HVO, and what his role was during the October conflict of 1992, the fact that he used his house, this so-called ignorance, it is a priori not credible at all. His claimed presence on the Radak Bridge calls for a number of observations. We received the testimony of Ivo Vidovic for the Defence, who saw Dragan Papic arriving at around 6.30, not from Ahmici, but from Rovna, and we also heard the testimony of Zvonimir Santic. Both of them, Ivo Vidovic and Zvonimir Santic, said that they were there on very strict orders, which included the fact that they should in no way move away from the Radak Bridge. Apparently, those men, those two witnesses in particular, as well as the accused, who went with them, on the 16th of April, in the first light of the morning, had become soldiers, but during the proceedings the Defence witnesses did not resolve the question as to whether one could say when they become soldiers. When did Nenad Santic find himself in a position to give orders to Dragan Papic? We remember the testimony of the younger brother of the accused, Goran Papic, who said that Dragan, with his family, had fled into the forest, which is right next to his house, and that he had then taken the women of the family to Rovna through -- across the Radak Bridge. And when he came back, he would take up his guard again. According to the witness, it was not that morning, the 16th of April, that his brother could have met Nenad Santic and received the order that he carried out. We must therefore consider that even if the witness Goran Papic's credibility appears more than suspect, if Dragan Papic, as the Defence claims, received the instruction to set up the guard, those instructions could only have been given to him before; not that morning, but before that, probably the day before the attack of the 16th of April. It is possible that the accused spent some of that day and the following days -- that is, a part of the 16th of April and the following days -- on the Radak Bridge but, as has been established by the Prosecution witnesses, that he was in the middle of the village on the 16th of April and on site for the killings, and that that cannot be a question, as was Husein Ahmic and the family of Witness G. Therefore, the Prosecution believes that it has demonstrated that the accused had associated himself with the nationalistic cause of the Bosnian Croats; that he was a member of the HVO forces, whatever the legal basis for that association; that he was part of a chain of command; and that he was, by necessity, informed about what was going to happen; that he had evacuated his family; and that on the 16th of April, 1993, he was present in uniform with a weapon in Ahmici. And the Prosecutor asks the Tribunal to find him guilty of count number 1, that is, persecution. Let me now move to the accused Drago Josipovic. The Prosecution believes that it has demonstrated that he had real nationalistic commitment, even though by temperament he is less expressive than Dragan. But his name is among the list of members of the HDZ and he's got family connections which connect him to members of the HVO, even if that does not implicate him directly, and therefore that sets up a context we cannot ignore. In the same way, his involvement in the armed units of the HVO has been established. We can remember that the accused mentioned on the HVO register for the period 8 October 1992 to the 15th of October 1995, he is mentioned as reservist, and the fact that he signed that -- signed that document, I don't believe was contested. As regards his involvement in the attack of the 16th of April against the Ahmici Muslim civilians, I would bring out several factors to be taken into consideration. Firstly, it is not contested that the accused, on the 16th of April, in the morning, was wearing a uniform, was carrying a weapon outside his house when the firing began, when the attack began. Many witnesses, both for the Defence and for the Prosecution, have reported that fact. We do not know through the Defence witnesses what led Drago Josipovic to leave his house in the early morning of the 16th of April before the attack began, wearing a uniform and carrying a weapon, whereas he claimed that he didn't know anything about what was going to happen. We do not know from the Defence witnesses what led him to join up with the Witness DG and what made him go to the location where the firing was coming from at the time that the attack began. But we are led, of course, to conclude that Drago Josipovic knew what was going to happen and that he was outside, wearing a uniform and with a weapon, before it began. That meant that he had the intention to participate in it. When he joined up with Witness DG, his family was in a shelter, and it might have been Rovna, but we don't know how the family got there or when it went. Witness Z has also stated that in the afternoon of 16 April, around 16 hours 30, he was alongside the main road. He saw Drago Josipovic at the head of four men along the edge of the road, all wearing camouflage units, all carrying automatic weapons, and that given the fact that the witness knew the accused very, very well, there is no possibility of error or confusion possible, because that group of soldiers was about 20 metres from him. That same Witness Z also declared before the Trial Chamber that shortly before getting into the UNPROFOR vehicle, he saw a certain -- a person named Aladin Karodzha, who was in the Ogrjev business and was waving to him from the other side of the road. The witness Kujawinski, a Sergeant in BritBat, took a photograph of those moments and confirmed that at the time that some of the refugees were getting into the BritBat vehicle, he saw a very frightened young man, who was able to get out of the Ogrjev building, after having tried to open the door of the building without succeeding, and so he was able to get through by climbing -- by crawling under it. We know that this Aladin Karodzha, who has since deceased, later on had the occasion of telling under what circumstances he had found himself locked up in the Ogrjev building. Witness BB, who, like Witness Z, was getting into one of the UNPROFOR vehicles, said that Aladin Karodzha told him that Drago Josipovic had locked him up in the building while he was accompanied with -- that they cut off the telephone lines and had threatened him. Another element to be evaluated by the Tribunal is that it has to do with the soldiers acting in that part of Ahmici came from his house. We know through the statement of Witness CA and by the statement of Witness CB, which shows us that the accused, when he left his house on the 16th of April in the morning, could not not have seen those soldiers or could not not have understood what was going to happen if he had not been otherwise informed. It also appeared during the proceedings that women and children, elderly people, who were Muslims, were detained during that day of the 16th of April, 1993 in Witness DG's house before being transferred to the Dubravica school. And we were able to see that the accused Drago Josipovic participated actively in that detention of refugees who were Muslims. The Defence, of course, tried to bring out the fact that this grouping of Muslims in a house was -- had been carried out for humanitarian, charitable reasons. But in fact we notice that these Muslims were put into a single house, and only that house and not in another one, and that these Muslims in that house were faced with extremely difficult conditions, according to Witness DG. Thirty-eight people were put together in two nine-square-metre rooms. The refugee said, the witness, I quote, "Were standing up like wooden matchsticks, one next to the other." Witness DG and Drago Josipovic were present in that house during the day of the 16th, as well as on the 17th of April, that is, the next day. They would come into the house, they would ask for people to -- men were there in order to come out, in order to go collect bodies. According to Witness CA, they deferred to their orders. Nenad Santic also came to that house. The next morning, that is, the 17th of April, everybody who had been collected in there were transferred to Zume to another house, and then on the next day they would be transferred to the Dubravica school. So that when they were in Zume, four people were called by the soldiers and then disappeared forever. Drago Josipovic accompanied the transfer of those Muslim refugees. He refused the Witness CA, who had wanted to stay, refusing the right to go back to his house. It is possible that some refugees, some Muslim refugees in the house, did not have the feeling that they were being detained, and some of them in fact might have even considered that after the hell of the -- that they experienced in the beginning of the morning, was now a refuge. But we saw that they simply did not have a choice, and that is what Witness CB told us: We did not have any other solution. That's all. Therefore, this house was a detention centre, a transit detention centre, and the accused Drago Josipovic played an active role in the detention of those individuals. And it is clear that by doing so he played an active role in the HVO operations, which demonstrates a very clear and established character of persecution. And now I move to the statement of Witness DD. Her son, her husband were killed, executed, while Drago Josipovic was present, according to the testimony. The witness stated, and you will remember, Your Honours, in what circumstances her 15-year-old son and her husband had been taken by the soldiers and executed. She stated that Drago Josipovic was on site when the events occurred. She claimed that she saw her face -- his face, sorry, especially so when at a given moment Drago Josipovic lifted his balaclava in order to wipe his forehead. She said that on two occasions she heard his voice. The first time when the witness was fighting with a soldier, Drago Josipovic intervened and ordered the soldiers to leave her alone. It appears that Drago Josipovic was then in the situation of command over the soldiers together with him. A second time she heard his voice when she was taken to the barn. She was locked in the barn and she heard his voice telling the soldiers coming from a neighbouring house belonging to the Croats that she should be saved. There again Drago is in a position of command over the soldiers who are with him. Lastly, I shall refer to the testimony of Witness EE. In referring to this testimony, I refer to charges against Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic. We shall remember the testimony of Witness EE. We know that the witness's house was very close to the accused's house. We remember that Witness EE recognised among the attackers who came to the witness's house, among those people, Vladimir Santic and Drago Josipovic, who were both, like the other soldiers, dressed in camouflage uniforms. Vladimir Santic, according to the witness, was then wearing a helmet. And there was another person named Zeljo Livancic. We know that person. He took the husband away and the witness is never to see her husband ever again. The witness stated that in the moments following the event when she left her house, which is then being torched, she must have had dealings with the accused Drago Josipovic, who told her where she had to go, and she had to deal also with Vladimir Santic, whom she saw passing by three metres away from her. At dusk she saw Drago Josipovic once more in uniform and armed, as well as Witness DG and DH. Witness EE identified Drago Josipovic in Court. She saw him very closely, she said, on several occasions on the 16th and the 17th of April. He was there where her husband was taken to and killed, and she also saw him during the attack. She said that she'd known him for a long time and that therefore there was no way she could have made a mistake or confused him for another person. Equally, she identified Vladimir Santic, whom she saw on two occasions within a very short distance on that morning. And she knew that person very well. According to the Prosecution, as to the main aspects of her testimony, the witness showed that she was a credible witness. It is our submission that of course it is up to the Trial Chamber to assess the witness's credibility and testimony. We know that her statement is being challenged by the Defence, which brings out mainly that she mentioned three people who could not possibly be present, according to the Defence, on the 16th of April. I have in mind Stipo Alilovic, Zeljo Livancic and Marinko Katava. The only thing I want to stress as regards Stipo Alilovic is that no evidence has been adduced during the trial, especially not by the Defence witnesses. It has not been established therefore that Stipo Alilovic, who was together with his family in Amsterdam and had been there since March '92, it was not established by the Defence that that man could not have left Holland to go back to Bosnia in the beginning of '93, especially around April '93. The Tribunal will assess this element, as well as the scope and the relevance of Witness CD's statement. Witness CD said here that Marinko Katava was in Vitez on the 16th of April, around 5.30, and the witness said that they saw this man again later in the day. We shall not go into further speculations; however, we maintain that as regarding Zeljo Livancic, we have gathered enough evidence, which came also from Defence witnesses, to establish that in a very likely way, almost certainly, Zeljo Livancic was present on the morning of the 16th of April in Ahmici and was involved in the attack carried out by the HVO against the civilian population of Ahmici. At any rate, with regard to the points I have just mentioned, the credibility of Witness EE is not challenged. With regard to Drago Josipovic, we have specific evidence, corroborating evidence. We have shown that, through his involvement, he had a personal and active part in the action and operations carried out against civilians in Ahmici. He had a very active and personal commitment and participation in the illegal detention of Muslims and also in the murder of the husband of Witness EE. He was present on-site when members of Witness DD's family were taken away and executed. From the testimony of witnesses, it appears that Drago Josipovic was fully aware of why he was there, he was fully aware of the fate of Witness EE and Witness DD's family members, and that, therefore, in full knowledge, he contributed to the achievement of the criminal intention of the attackers. I am now moving to speak about the accused Vladimir Santic. Obviously, he is different from the other accused, in as much as he's not a resident of Ahmici on the one hand, and on the other hand, at the time, at the relevant times, he has very relevant military duties and responsibilities. He has a commanding role which has been established and demonstrated and was not challenged by the Defence. I am of the opinion that we can conclude that this career police officer, HVO military police member, was a commander of the 4th Company of the military police battalion since 1993, including the anti-terrorist platoon called the Jokers. Many witnesses heard in court, many documents tendered into evidence, have demonstrated the military commanding role played by Vladimir Santic. I especially refer to the testimony of Witness AA, who was a subordinate of the accused and who stated to this Court that Vladimir Santic was a very strict commander, had a very tight grip over the units under his orders, and especially so over the unit which was to be called the Jokeri, or Jokers. Also, the accused acknowledged that Anto Furundzija was the leader of the Jokers. According to Witness AA, it was proved that Anto Furundzija, the head of the Jokeri platoon, could not act if he did not have the approval or the orders of Vladimir Santic, who was the company commander, and that Vladimir Santic was very, very close to his men and also was to be seen in the Bungalow. On the basis of such facts, and to corroborate them, we have some of the written orders issued by Vladimir Santic. I refer to Exhibit 390. We also have, and this is important, we have the evidence showing that Vladimir Santic exerted disciplinary powers over his men whenever he thought that necessary or suitable. We also know that following -- before the 16th of April, as well as on the 16th of April, Vladimir Santic was present, he was seen in the Bungalow, together with his men belonging to the Jokeri unit. We equally know that Vladimir Santic did not carry out his command responsibilities in an impartial way, with the necessary concern that he should have had regarding his public duties. He was described by Witness AA as very indulgent, if not absolutely passive, in the face of serious crimes and repeated crimes, such as looting and burglaries committed at the expense of the Muslims, often by members of his unit. We shall remember the very serious incident of the arrest of Miroslav Bralo, who was accused of killing Sakic. Bralo was arrested, detained for some time at the Kaonik prison in comfortable conditions, and he was then released with the passive or active cooperation of Vladimir Santic. Let us speak about the part played by the Jokeri during the day in Ahmici. It was established by testimony, not only of victims of the attack -- we have heard Abdulah Ahmic, Witness A, Witness E, F, C, A, and GG -- but also by members of the BritBat who entered Ahmici or passed by the Bungalow on that day. I refer to the testimony of Andre Kujawinski, who saw in front of the Bungalow on that afternoon many soldiers drinking and rejoicing, and he thought that they were involved in the attack carried out on Ahmici. We also remember the testimony of Lee Whitworth, who later came across men from the Bungalow and who had the feeling that, implicitly, the Jokers claimed the authorship and their victory, their so-called military victory over Ahmici. Vlado Santic was present in Ahmici, together with this man. That has been established as well beyond any reasonable doubt, particularly so by the submissions or by the observations of Asim Dzambasovic, by referring to the principles which govern the functioning of armies in all the countries of the world, explaining that a platoon leader, such as Anto Furundzija, can address his hierarchy only through his company commander and that all orders given to a platoon can only be done so through the company commander. The company commander also has the duty to watch over the good execution of the orders he gives and that, for that purpose, he has to be on the ground with his men. Starting from these elementary principles applicable in all armies, we must conclude, first, that the illegal orders were given to the Jokers; secondly, that those orders were given by or through the intermediary of the accused Vlado Santic and, of course, that there may be no written trace of them; thirdly, that a company commander can only accompany his men on the ground, which means that in this case, he had to be physically present on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici. Consequently, in view of his responsibilities as the leader of the 1st Company of the 4th Military Police Battalion, Vlado Santic was closely involved in facts of persecution and ethnic cleansing of Muslim civilians of Ahmici. He gave the orders; that is, at least if he received general directives, he transmitted them, in spite of their clearly illegal character, and completed the orders for the implementation. But his contribution is even greater because the accused was present on the 16th of April, early in the morning, in front of the house of Witness EE and together with his men. I have already reviewed the testimony of Witness EE, and I will not go back to it, but I wish just to refer, concerning the role of Vlado Santic, that the statements of Witness EE were corroborated, first, by the fact that Witness CA reported that Witness EE, as soon as he arrived in the collection and detention centre, mentioned the name of the accused Vladimir Santic as being one of the persons that she saw near her house at the moment that her husband was killed; secondly, Witness CB, called by the Defence, also said in a clear and formal manner that she remembered that Witness EE mentioned, on the 16th of April, the name of Vlado Santic, who came in front of her door and who refused to answer her question when Witness EE asked, "What are you doing here, Vlado?" A last element of evidence which I should like to submit, the Prosecution has submitted a video film, Exhibit 253; it is a film made around the Bungalow, and on this film, we see the accused. Witness AA recognised categorically the place where the film was shot, that is, the Bungalow, and formally identified the accused Vladimir Santic. As noted on the film itself, it was taken on the 16th of April, in the evening. We know that the Defence witness Biletic said that he saw the accused in the Bungalow, surrounded by his men, on the 16th of April. In view of the charges against the accused, I do not believe that the Defence was able to prove the alibi that it alleged to be supported by Witness Ivica Franjic and Davor Biletic. Ivica Franjic spoke of the presence of the accused in Vitez at 6.30, and in view of the short distance between Vitez and Ahmici, this did not prevent him from being, at the beginning of the attack, in front of the witness's house. As for Witness Davor Biletic, I draw attention to the inconsistencies and certain odd moments of his testimony which have to be viewed with great precaution. If the witness was present in the Hotel Vitez, which he remembers, he is supposed to have forgotten everything else that happened that morning and all the circumstances of that day. Consequently, I do not think that Davor Biletic can be in a position to contribute useful testimony to the Court and, above all, that his testimony is not sufficient to discredit the evidence of the Prosecution. Therefore, I ask the Court to find Vladimir Santic to be guilty, by the orders he gave and the responsibilities he had and the personal actions he committed, for Counts 1 and Counts 16 to 19. I said at the beginning of my closing statement, Mr. President and Your Honours, that the Prosecution wanted to say what they thought should be the penalties handed down to each of the accused. In view of the limited time I have left, and the time for the questions, I refer you to the written submission of the Prosecution regarding the criteria that should be taken into account when determining the sanctions that should be handed down to each of the accused. As regards Dragan Papic, Dragan Papic, was he the person that Captain Stevens recognised on the 21st of April, 1993, his satisfaction that he expressed for the death of the Muslims? I wish simply to underline that, in view of the evidence against him, his character, his fanatic commitment, the fact is, to say the least, plausible. For the period prior to the massacre and the 16th of April, 1993, the accused was zealously involved in HVO activities, intimidating the Muslim population of Ahmici, contributing significantly to the increase of tensions and insecurity. He lent his house to the attacker, which turned it into a logistics base and a kind of headquarters. He was active. He executed orders given to him by the HVO command. He was present where the killings took place. But the Prosecution bears in mind the fact that no specific killing has been attributed to him. Therefore, the Prosecution recommends a penalty of around eight years of imprisonment. Vlatko Kupreskic, I don't think that we will know truly what was the extent of his role and his real involvement in the actions of the HVO. At least we know, without any doubt, that he was not an honest businessman, totally preoccupied with his business, as he pretends to be. The Prosecution has shown his relationships with the HVO; that he was necessarily associated with the preparations for the attack and that he actively contributed, without any risk to the success of the attacker; that he gave assistance, at least material assistance, allowing the use of his house; that he was together with other soldiers and he personally shot at a group of Muslims consisting of women, children, and elderly; and that he was a co-perpetrator of the death of a mother and a young girl. We, therefore, recommend the penalty of around 12 years' imprisonment. Zoran Kupreskic, who claims to be devoted to peace between the communities; however, the evidence of the Tribunal shows that he was, in fact, far from neutral. Quite to the contrary. He was actively involved in favour of the Croatian cause, and he had a role of responsibility. He took no steps to warn his neighbours and friends, Muslims, to save them, and a few months before, he signed a request demanding them to disarm and guaranteeing their security. The Prosecution has established that he took an active and, perhaps, a determining role in the aggression of the 16th of April, and, as Witness JJ said, if he had any remorse, he did not convey it to the Judges. But he knows what he did, and according to the view of the Prosecution, he killed, persecuted, without even wishing to save two children. The killing of those two children is not only the product of ethnic cleansing but logic, to cut the line of generation. If the Judges of the Tribunal have been convinced by the evidence of the Prosecution regarding the responsibility of the accused, the Prosecution recommends a penalty which should not be less than 20 years of imprisonment. The Prosecution submits that the involvement of Mirjan Kupreskic is equal to that of his brother Zoran. He was closely associated with the HVO forces and shared their military and political objectives. Like his brother, he did not warn his friends, not even his best friend Fahrudin. When he entered the house, Witness KL, accompanied by his brother, he knows what to -- what he would find because he knew all the members of that family and he didn't spare anyone, not even the children. But the Prosecution will understand that the Tribunal may consider that the accused was under the influence of his brother, who was older and more instructed and had a high degree of responsibility in the HVO command. If the Tribunal shares the view of the Prosecution regarding the position of this accused, the Prosecution recommends a penalty that will not be less than 15 years of imprisonment. As regards Drago Josipovic, we know by his family surroundings and also by conviction that the accused was closely linked to the HVO authorities from the very first hours of the Bosnian Croat adventure. He was necessarily involved in the attack, the preparation of the attack, and clearly also in the execution of that attack. He was present when a number of killings took place. He was the co-perpetrator of two killings, one of a young adolescent. According to the testimony heard, he had a position of authority and influence over the people in his -- together with him. He took part in the detention of more than 30 Muslims thrown out of their houses and deported outside their village. The Prosecution recommends a penalty of around 15 years of imprisonment. Vladimir Santic, among all the accused, has the greatest criminal responsibility. A man of authority, of experience and power. He was necessarily and closely involved in the preparation of the attack and in its execution. His position of command, his hierarchical position, indicates that he was perfectly aware as to what would happen. He was fully conscious of his role. He was present on the 16th of April with his men in Ahmici. He headed them and thus encouraged them. He was also present with his men after the 16th of April, thereby approving their acts. And as a former police officer, knowing the law and the characteristics of crimes, he is in a better position than any of the accused to be aware of the criminal nature of his behaviour, and the criminal nature of the behaviour of the men that participated in the attack. The Prosecution recommends a penalty of around 30 years of imprisonment. I would now like to say some very brief concluding words. We can remember at the very beginning of this trial we showed a video, and in the video you could see a British soldier, an anonymous British soldier, who was in Ahmici when some of the charred bodies were discovered. And he expresses indignation, his disgust, and his protest when he said, "This is 1993, not 1943." And these words are perhaps the strongest and most violent of those that we heard throughout this trial. But it is not only the observation of that soldier which takes us back to the past. We have a great many echoes in this trial of what happened in that region of Europe about 50 years ago. Whether it be the 16th of April of 1941 when Ante Pavelic went back to Zagreb from his exile in Italy in order to take over the leadership of the sinister enterprise of the Ustashes, that may be a coincidence. But it is obviously significant that the HVO Zenica brigade took the name of Jure Francetic. Defence witness Jadranka Tolic, a member of that brigade, said that Francetic was a historical person under whose patronage they had placed themselves, but he said he did not know anything further than that. It is well-known that Francetic was the head of an Ustashes unit known as the Black unit, which sowed terror in eastern Bosnia through its acts against the civilian populations. In fact, by showing this same hegemonic resolve, the same nationalistic and historical references, the same resolve to appropriate territories exclusively of violence of the same type, the same content for individuals belonging to other communities, some Bosnian Croats, and I am saying not all of the Bosnian Croats, some of them connected those two periods of history of 1943 and 1993. Justice was not rendered against those responsible for the Ustashes crimes. So that history not repeat itself, we have this Tribunal. Thank you Mr. President. I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. I am sure that you are very tired, but I would like to ask you a question about a problem which was pointed out by the Defence. In the brief which you filed last week, accused Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, among other things, of the murder of the father of Witness H. And perhaps you would remember that on the 3rd of September I had asked that same question of your colleague Mr. Moskowitz when I asked him whether the Prosecution was going to bring charges, a specific charge that is, against the two accused in respect of that murder. And at that time Mr. Moskowitz said, "Yes, we had thought about bringing a specific charge, but we decided not to ask that the indictment be amended. In any case, you will take into account the evidence that we have presented." And I have in front of me the relevant pages of the transcript. These are pages 1.696 FF. And he added, "And you must decide to what extent one could take into account that evidence as regards persecution." All right. Now, here is my question: What is your position now about that murder? I repeat. In the written brief you accused the two accused of that murder, which, however, does not appear officially, in the indictment. To what extent can the Tribunal take into account the charges that were not actually formulated in an official way in the indictment itself, but which were put forth during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will answer you analogously as -- like the way Mr. Moskowitz said for the Prosecution, and which you've just recalled. It is true that the murder of Witness H's father is not in the indictment. It is true that the evidence, at least this is the point of view of the Prosecution, that the evidence that was presented to the Tribunal shows that most probably one or the other of the accused, Zoran and Mirjan, both of them were near it when that happened. But we do not say that they themselves are the perpetrators of that murder. We do not know who were the ones who killed Witness H's father. However, we do know that the two accused, according to the Prosecution evidence, were there. Therefore, according to the point of view that I am expressing today, it seems to me that it is pursuant to the charge of persecution that this aspect of the -- both of their behaviours can be taken into account, the behaviour in front of Witness H's house, not as a specific crime which could be ascribed to them personally, but we have a more reliable source, and this is the point of view of the Prosecution, is that they were in the house a few moments after Witness H's father was murdered, and the exchange that took place there between the two accused and the Witness H. Therefore, my answer to the question, Mr. President, goes back to the one which was already given to you by Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, very well. Well, let me ask you another question then. Therefore, you are suggesting that we take into account, assuming that the Trial Chamber is convinced by the Prosecution evidence, that you want this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, more specifically, the Prosecution suggests to the Trial Chamber to take into account, pursuant to Count number 1, persecution, the behaviour of the accused, in front of and inside Witness H's house, as it appeared through the Prosecution's evidence, which the Tribunal, of course, will evaluate. Once again, we cannot state -- we know that Witness H's father was shot, was executed on that location at that time, in front of his house. We also know that the accused, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, were a few metres away from there, but we do not know any more about what their role was in that execution. However, we do know through Witness H what their role was in Witness H's house, and lastly, pursuant to persecutions that were carried out against that family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We still have a few moments left. I have a few other questions. I just ask one that has to do with what you said today about the attack -- the armed attack and the lack of resistance on the part of the Muslims. You added or, rather, you noted that there were two Croats who were wounded and another Croat, a Croatian soldier who was killed. There was also testimony here, speaking about the fact that they fired -- that they were participants in at least a certain number of combat activities. How can you explain that there was this minimum number of exchange of rifle fire and between a group of armed civilians and the Croatian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What the Prosecution is saying about this question, Mr. President, is as follows: We do not preclude the fact that some of the inhabitants -- the Muslim inhabitants in Ahmici who might have had personal weapons did not put up some degree of resistance against the attack in order to protect their homes and their families. We do know specifically what I believe we were told by Witness V. We do not preclude the fact that some type of resistance was put forth against the aggressor, but we do say that any resistance was very localised; that it was the result of civilians who were attempting to protect their property and their families. It did not last, that is the resistance did not last, and that in the end it really did not prevent anything in that attack. Perhaps it delayed things by a few moments near Grabovi, but it did not prevent anything. As regards the Croatian victims, we know through HVO documents, not through testimony, Prosecution testimony, but HVO documents that two people who lived in Ahmici and who were members of the Vitez Brigade battalion were wounded during that action. We have no other details as to the circumstances in which they were wounded, of course. We were told that the person named Mirjan Santic was killed. We have no documentary evidence about the fact that the death took place in Ahmici on that day, aside from a book which has been devoted to the glory of the military police of the HVO. The official documents do not mention the death of Marijan Santic in Ahmici that day. But we do not exclude the possibility that this may have taken place. In any case, if it did take place, it is through personal resistance carried out by several citizens, resistance which was not organised, which was spot specific. It did not last, and which did not prevent anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can now adjourn. And we'll see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.28 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of November, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
